claims.overstatement: None. The claim keeps association language where Broyd writes 'impaired' throughout; 'nothing pooled' is correct (qualitative synthesis of 105 studies).
claims.note: All Broyd numbers recovered from Table 1 (chronic column): verbal learning and memory +++ (20), attention +++ (14), working memory +- (16), planning-type executive functions +- (23), inhibition +- (9), decision making +- (17), psychomotor + (10). '+++' is defined as strong and largely consistent evidence of impairment, and the footnote says the ratings are the authors' subjective consensus. 'More than half ... did not report IQ or education' matches 'more than 50% of studies' (AM p. 9). The frequency sentence (AM p. 8) cites the senior author's own earlier review (ref 20). Broyd's chronic samples span adolescents to adults aged about 35-50 and include occasional users in one study (ref 55), so they are broader than the claim's 'adolescents and young adults'; the claim attributes the ratings to 'people who use cannabis regularly', which is fair.

claims.overstatement: None; Curran is not named in the statement.
claims.note: Curran agrees that long-term memory impairments are reported mainly with frequent, heavy use and that confounding prevents causal conclusions (p. 297; Conclusions p. 302). It differs from Broyd on attention: Curran calls findings for working memory, attention and impulsivity mixed (p. 297), whereas the claim reports Broyd's rating of attention as strong and largely consistent; a clause noting that a narrative review of the same year calls attention findings mixed would show the disagreement.

claims.overstatement: Slight: calling all 16 'memory, speed and executive tests' makes the result look broader within those domains than it is (7 of 14), and the 16 tests were not corrected for multiple comparisons. The claim's closing caution (no comparison can show causation) fits this source.
claims.note: Exposure (number of the five interviews from 18 to 38 at which dependence criteria were met, as a five-level score whose lowest two levels separate never-users from people who used but were never dependent), adjustment (childhood full-scale IQ and sex) and 'not given in childhood' all match. The count 9 of 16 matches Table 3, but the 16 scores are 5 executive, 6 memory, 3 processing-speed, 1 perceptual-reasoning and 1 verbal-comprehension score; 2 of the 9 significant ones are the WAIS-IV Perceptual Reasoning and Verbal Comprehension indexes, so the memory, speed and executive tests alone give 7 of 14. Suggested wording: '9 of 16 tests of memory, speed, executive function, reasoning and verbal comprehension'. All 9 go in the direction of poorer scores; none of the 5 time or error scores (higher = worse) was significant. No correction for multiple testing is reported (editors' calculation: at 0.05/16 = 0.003, 3 of 16 remain: Months of the Year Backward, Processing Speed Index, Verbal Comprehension Index). The authors' test that the four WAIS-IV index associations could be set equal (chi-square change 2.13, df = 3, P = 0.55) means no domain stood out.

claims.overstatement: None. One imprecision: 'scored lower than the others on 4 of 6 executive-function scores' should be 'performed worse on'. One of the four is SWM Strategy, where higher scores are worse and the dependent group scored higher (0.21 against −0.01).
claims.note: Checked: 84 of 1,989 (4.2%) with past-year DSM-IV dependence at 18, against the 1,902 to 1,905 without; worse on 4 of 6 CANTAB scores (RVP A prime, SWM Strategy, Spatial Span Forward and Reversed) and on 2 (the spatial spans) after age-12 IQ; no differences in the 57 discordant pairs; Spatial Span Forward −0.48 against 0.02 in the full sample and −0.38 against −0.18 (t −1.30, p = .20) in the pairs; sex-adjusted z-scores. Worth adding: with frequency of use as the exposure, the twin who used more often did worse than the co-twin on Spatial Span Reversed (beta −0.07, p = .036; .022 after age-12 IQ; 974 pairs), the one within-pair difference, which the authors say may be a false positive. In the full sample, frequency went with worse performance on 5 of 6 tests after age-12 IQ. The tests cover attention/vigilance and spatial working memory only, with no memory tests. Use was mostly light (63% none in the past year, 28% less than monthly, 1% many times a day).

claims.overstatement: Minor. (1) 'The difference depended on how recently people had used': the moderator is each study's minimum required abstinence (not measured recency), and the authors describe the abstinence associations as holding at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons; 'was smaller in studies that required longer abstinence' would be exact. (2) The statement names visuospatial and motor as showing no clear difference but omits verbal/language (-0.14, 95% CI -0.27 to 0.001, P = .05), also non-significant (it is in the magnitude). (3) 'samples of people seeking treatment differed more' rests on an uncorrected P = .04 (said in the magnitude, not in the statement). (4) 'raw test scores': the authors say their analyses 'primarily' used raw scores; some studies supplied normed scores. None changes the claim's meaning.
claims.note: All Scott numbers in statement and magnitude match the text. Editors' approximate 95% prediction interval recomputed: -0.247 +/- 1.96 x sqrt(0.070 + 0.038^2) = -0.771 to +0.277, i.e. -0.77 to +0.28 (same; with t on 67 df, -0.78 to +0.29). Trim-and-fill reduction recomputed (0.206 - 0.128)/0.206 = 37.9%, as printed. CI from SE: -0.247 +/- 1.96 x 0.038 = -0.32 to -0.17 (same). '69 cross-sectional samples' is a fair label: the paper calls them 69 studies, but several papers contribute two rows to the Table (e.g. Fried 2005, Tait 2011, Schweinsburg 2010). Also noted: subgroup k for treatment-seeking (12) and non-treatment-seeking (56) sums to 68, not 69, while their n (581 + 8146) sums to the full 8727.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of Broyd. If anything the Broyd sentences understate the review's own lean toward persistence: they report Table 1's 'mixed' persistence ratings and the authors' suggestion that verbal memory may recover, but not the abstract (AM p. 3) or Table 2 (AM p. 26), which give likely persistent effects on attention and psychomotor function and possible persistent effects on verbal learning and memory. Table 1 itself rates attention persistence as mixed, so the review is internally inconsistent here; the claim's 'contested' status covers it.
claims.note: Every Broyd number in the statement and magnitude was recovered: 2004-2015 (January 2004 to February 2015); eighteen abstinence studies (more than 24 h), most often 21-35 days, few longer; eleven cross-sectional (7 days to more than 1 year; 9 in adolescents or young adults) and seven prospective (21 days to 4-8 years; two confounded by drug treatment); Table 1 persistence +- for verbal learning and memory (9), working memory (7), attention (10), planning-type executive functions (9), verbal fluency (4), + for psychomotor (6), - for other memory (4), time estimation (1) and decision making (3). '23 to 53 days' maps to refs 91 (23 days, adults), 65 (28 days), 67 (35 days) and 85 (53 days; working memory and risk taking); 'older adults abstinent more than 28 days' is ref 57 (AM p. 10 says >28 days, AM p. 7 says >=28 days, aged about 35-50). The adolescent prospective study is ref 79 (Fried 2005) and the 12-month cohort ref 66 (Tait 2011). Table 1's abstinence column cites 17 distinct studies against 18 in the text. Broyd presents Meier 2012 as IQ decline persisting after cessation or reduction of use in the past year (AM p. 10) and says cessation did not restore IQ (AM p. 9); the claim correctly declines that reading. The 'critically low' AMSTAR 2 label is the editors' rating, not Broyd's; it is consistent with what the main text shows (no protocol, two databases, no formal appraisal of included studies; search details only in Supplement 1).

claims.overstatement: None. The claim reports Curran's 'converging to show' statement as Curran's, names its two citations and correctly says the receptor finding is not a test of cognition.
claims.note: Curran's two citations for the 4-6 weeks statement are ref 58 (Pope et al., 2001, a single study) and ref 59 (Schreiner & Dunn, 2012, a meta-analysis); 'about 4 weeks of monitored abstinence' is Hirvonen et al. (2012, ref 30): '~4 weeks of continuously monitored abstinence' in a secure research unit, with cortical CB1 receptor density back to control levels. Not in the claim, all pointing the same way: Curran adds that one recent study (D'Souza et al., 2016, ref 31) found receptor recovery after as little as 2 days (p. 298), and says on p. 297, citing a review (Crane et al., 2013), that some studies find deficits in the first few days of abstinence but little evidence of deficits at 28 days. Against this, Box 1 (p. 294) describes the Dunedin decline as still apparent in people using less than once a week at 38, the reading the claim corrects from Meier et al. (2012).

claims.overstatement: None as to strength: the claim rightly says this is not a test of abstinence. The exposure is misdefined (see note).
claims.note: Numbers check against Fig. 3: 17 people, p = .03, use weekly or less in the year before the age-38 test, median 14 days (range 0-52), childhood about 102 to adult about 97.5 (my reading 102.2 to 97.5). Error in the exposure: Fig. 3 is restricted to people with dependence at 2 or more of the five interviews and splits them by onset of at least weekly cannabis use before 18 (panel label: used cannabis weekly before age 18), not by onset of dependence before 18. 'Persistent dependence that began in adolescence' (statement) and 'adolescent-onset persistent dependence' (magnitude) should read, for example, 'people with dependence at two or more interviews who had used cannabis weekly before 18'. The paper does not say what test gives p = .03 (a within-group childhood-to-adult comparison). There is no never-user comparison in this analysis. Frequent adolescent-onset users (n = 19) fell more (about 96.8 to 89.2, p = .0002), and neither adult-onset group changed significantly (p = .73 and .11). The authors describe these people as having quit or reduced use for a year or more (Discussion, 2nd and 4th paragraphs), which goes beyond the figure's definition (up to 52 days of use in that year, self-reported); the claim's 'not a test of abstinence' is the right reading. The Fig. 3 groups total 69, against 73 people with 2 or more waves of dependence in Table 1, with no explanation given.

claims.overstatement: One clause is contradicted by the source's own numbers: the >72 h subgroup's 95% CI is -0.22 to 0.07, so it includes no difference but does NOT include the overall difference of -0.25 (-0.247); the two intervals overlap (-0.22 to -0.17), but the overall point estimate lies just outside the subgroup interval. Suggested wording: 'the interval includes no difference and reaches -0.22, close to the overall -0.25'. Second, '7 of the 15 longer-abstinence studies come from papers by one research group': 7 is the count of rows whose printed reference names Tapert SF; an 8th (Jacobus et al. 2015, ref 62) shares its first two authors with Jacobus et al. 2014 but its printed author list stops at 'et al.', so 'at least 7' is the safe wording. Third, P = .01 is given without 'uncorrected', although the authors describe the abstinence associations as holding 'albeit at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons' (Discussion) and about ten moderators were tested. The claim's overall conclusion (insufficient, disputed) is more cautious than the authors' own conclusion that abstinence beyond 72 h 'diminishes' deficits; given a between-study, cross-sectional comparison this caution is justified, not an understatement.
claims.note: Scott-derived numbers checked: -0.08 (-0.22 to 0.07), 15 studies, n = 928, P = .29; -0.30 (-0.37 to -0.22), 54 studies, n = 7799; chi-square 6.36, P = .01; beta 0.059, P = .04 uncorrected, k = 28 (n = 1661); mean required abstinence 152.7 h (SD 335.2); 22/32/15 studies; 14 monitored: all as printed. 7 to 90 days: confirmed from the Table (168 h to 2160 h). 11 of 15 with age ranges ending at 20 or younger: confirmed (the 4 exceptions: Fried 2005 17-21, Lisdahl & Price 2012 18-28, Murphy 2011 18-30, Price 2015 18-25). The -0.30 (-0.37 to -0.22) value for the 54 studies is printed in the Abstract only (the Results text gives only k, n, chi-square and P; Figure 3 not viewed). Table check: the 15 >72 h rows sum to 410 + 537 = 947 participants, not the 928 printed in the text (and the 54 other rows to 7814, not 7799); the claim correctly uses the text's figure. Two of the 15 'studies' are second rows of papers whose other row is in the <=72 h group (Fried 2005 at 0 h and 2160 h; Schweinsburg 2010 at 48 h and 648 h), so the subgroup contrast is not purely between independent studies, but it is never within the same people before and after stopping, as the claim says.

claims.overstatement: None in the claim. Broyd itself reads Meier 2012 causally ('resulted in', AM p. 10), says specificity was 'determined by ruling out' recent use and other substance use, and that cessation did not restore IQ, without the multivariable attenuation or the socioeconomic critique; the claim's 'insufficient' and 'disputed' are the more cautious reading.
claims.note: No number in the claim comes from Broyd. Broyd's '~6 points' for persistent use or dependence matches the claim's 99.68 to 93.93 (5.75 points, about 6) in the 38 people with dependence at 3 or more waves. Broyd does not quote the 8-point figure.

claims.overstatement: None; Curran is not named in the statement.
claims.note: Curran gives 'up to 6 IQ points' for persistent dependence (Box 1, p. 294) and 'around 8 IQ points' for dependence that began in adolescence and persisted (p. 298), consistent with the claim (99.68 to 93.93 = 5.75 points in the 38 people; -0.54 SD x 15 = about 8.1 points in the 23 with onset before 18). Curran's 1,037 is the cohort, not the 874 analysed. Two qualifiers the claim does not carry: Box 1 describes a third prospective cohort, the UK birth cohort of 2,235 adolescents aged 15-16 (Mokrysz et al., 2016, a study by one of Curran's co-authors), in which cumulative use was not associated with lower IQ after pre-teen IQ and confounders (notably tobacco and alcohol use) were taken into account, with only 72 reporting more than 50 uses; and Curran says the Dunedin cohort's older, lower-potency cannabis limits its relevance today (p. 294). Box 1's statement that all studies ignored residual effects on IQ testing is not accurate for Dunedin, which, as the claim says, left out recent use in a sensitivity analysis.

claims.overstatement: None in strength: the claim reports the co-twin results as 'did not differ significantly' with wide intervals, not as evidence of no effect, and does not adopt the authors' conclusion that the decline is due to confounding rather than cannabis. One clarity point: 'fell 4.0 and 3.4 points further behind age peers' is a difference in change between those who used and those who did not. On raw means, those who used fell 1.8 and 2.5 points while those who did not rose 1.8 and 1.3.
claims.note: Every number in the statement and magnitude checks against Tables 3, 5, S4 and S6: 789 and 2,277; −4.0 (−6.3 to −1.7) and −3.4 (−4.5 to −2.3); −3.7 (−6.8 to −0.5) and −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6) with binge drinking and other drug use; identical pairs −5.4 (−11.2 to 0.5; 25) and −0.7 (−3.9 to 2.4; 112); non-identical −2.8 (−7.7 to 2.2; 54) and 0.2 (−2.8 to 3.3; 99); 47 heavy-use pairs −1.5 (−5.5 to 2.6). Exposure (ever use on any occasion by follow-up against never), ages (9-12 to 17-20) and adjustment set (age, sex, race, zygosity, SES, MTFS cohort) match. The missing part: 'but not on four other subtests' leaves out the Information subtest. In the MTFS, the only cohort that gave it, those who used declined 2.0 points more (−3.3 to −0.7, P = 0.002), and the authors' main reading rests on Vocabulary and Information together. Six subtests were given in all: Vocabulary declined in both cohorts, Information in the one that gave it, and the other four (Similarities, Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Picture Arrangement) showed no difference. Information also fell to −0.7 (−2.3 to 0.9) after adjustment for drinking and other drugs. Suggested addition: 'and on Information (−2.0, −3.3 to −0.7; MTFS only)'. Smaller points: 'lower scores preceded use' holds for Vocabulary (−1.9), Information (−2.7) and Block Design (−2.0) at 11-12 in the MTFS, but there were no baseline differences in the RFAB. 'Intervals wide enough to include the between-family differences' holds for the identical pairs and the RFAB non-identical pairs; the MTFS non-identical interval (−2.8 to 3.3) excludes −3.4. Among those who used, use more than 30 times or daily use was not linked with more decline (Table 4). Half the later MTFS sample was recruited for disruptive behaviour. Attrition was high in the RFAB: 427 of 1,241 lacked cannabis data and had lower baseline IQ and SES, and 323 of 789 had no follow-up IQ. Table 5 has three P values that do not match their intervals (see the anchor); none changes significance.

claims.overstatement: None from this source: the claim keeps to association, reports the fall in the test statistic under fuller adjustment and attributes the 8 points to 23 people. One misstatement: 'with no test of the difference' (Fig. 2 prints p = .02).
claims.note: All Meier 2012 numbers check: 874 = 242 + 479 + 80 + 35 + 38; 38/874 = 4.3% (about 4 in 100); 81.58% male; 99.84 to 100.64 (+0.05 SD) and 99.68 to 93.93 (5.75 points, −0.38 SD; about 6, as the text says); t = −4.45 (sex-adjusted), −3.41 (education), −2.20 (multivariable; −2.20/−4.45 = 0.49, so 'about halved' holds); 7 cohort members had tried cannabis by 13; Fig. 2 read as −0.54 (n = 23) and −0.14 (n = 14). Corrections: (1) 'with no test of the difference' is contradicted by Fig. 2, which gives p = .02 for adolescent- against adult-onset dependence at 3 or more waves (p = .44 at 1 wave, .09 at 2); the paper does not say what test this is and reports no interaction test, so the statement could say 'p = .02 by a test the paper does not describe; not significant at 1 or 2 waves'. The magnitude already gives p = .02, so statement and magnitude disagree. (2) In the multivariable model 'recent use' is past-24-hour use only; past-week use was handled only by exclusion. (3) The magnitude labels the group change scores 'sex-adjusted', but each equals the raw mean change divided by 15 (Table 1), so they are unadjusted; only the trend tests are sex-adjusted. Not in the claim and worth knowing: the trend held without the 3+ group (t = −2.94); persistent regular use (4 or more days a week) gave a similar gradient (3+ waves, n = 41: 96.00 to 90.77, −0.35); the Fig. 2 groups (74, 33, 37) fall short of Table 1's (80, 35, 38) without explanation; no coefficient, standard error or interval is reported for any trend; the authors say causality cannot be established and that adjusting for education may be overcontrol.

claims.overstatement: None: the claim says IQ 'did not fall significantly more' and that discordant twins 'did not differ', with the editors' intervals, and does not adopt the authors' conclusion that short-term adolescent use 'does not appear to cause IQ decline'.
claims.note: All numbers check against Table 2 and Table 3: 1,989 tested at 5, 12 and 18; 84 against 1,905; sex-adjusted differences −5.23 (t −2.94, p = .003), −5.61 (t −3.11, p = .002) and −7.34 (t −5.27, p < .001); change 12 to 18, −1.81 against −0.08, difference −1.73 (t −1.27, p = .20); 57 discordant pairs: age 18 −1.45 (p = .42), change 0.05 (p = .98); frequency, change beta −0.05 (p = .035) and −0.02 within pairs (p = .46). The editors' intervals reproduce: −1.73 with SE 1.36 gives −4.4 to 0.9; −1.45 with SE 1.79 gives −5.0 to 2.1. Worth adding: 'IQ' here is a pro-rated estimate from two subtests (Vocabulary and Block Design at 5; Information and Matrix Reasoning at 12 and 18), standardized within the sample. The within-pair change estimate (0.05) has no interval, and its t is rounded to 0.02, so its precision cannot be recovered; with 57 pairs it cannot exclude a decline as large as the full-sample −1.73. After age-5 IQ, the full-sample change was −2.02 (t −1.49, p = .14). The frequency coefficients are standardized betas per SD of frequency, not IQ points. In the Discussion the authors describe their 2012 Dunedin finding as an 8-point decline 'from age 18-38', but the Dunedin baseline was childhood IQ at 7-13 (see the meier_2012 out file). That does not affect this claim.

claims.overstatement: Slight: 'did not predict adolescent-onset dependence' drops 'significantly'. The source reports a non-significant test (chi-square 1.15, P = 0.56) in a small group, which is not the same as no association. For IQ change, 'did not predict' is fair (r = −0.006 in the full cohort).
claims.note: All four coefficients check against the text: −0.152 (t −4.45, P < 0.0001; the published sex-adjusted model), −0.158 with SES (t −4.58), −0.151 with childhood self-control (t −4.38, P = 0.0001), and −0.155 in middle-class families only (t −3.61, P = 0.0003). Chi-square 1.15, P = 0.56 and r = −0.006 also check; P = 0.86 is not in the claim. Consistency checks: P = 0.56 matches a chi-square of 1.15 on 2 df (three SES groups), and r = −0.006 with about 870 people gives P of about 0.86. Not checked: the 553 people from middle-class families. That number is not in the text and must come from Fig. 2 or 3, which I could not view. A rough check from the printed beta and t (n ≈ 550 after scaling to the full-sample values) makes it plausible. Not stated in the source: whether beta is standardized. Points the claim could carry: SES and self-control were each added alone, never together or with the other dependence covariates; the middle-class analysis excludes high- as well as low-SES families; SES is the breadwinner's occupation; the reply shows no IQ trajectories before use by exposure group (Fig. 1 is IQ by SES); and the authors' wording ('actual data exclude the possibility', 'these tests exclude') is stronger than single-covariate adjustment allows. The claim does not repeat that wording.

claims.overstatement: None. 'Showed that ... could produce' fits a simulation that shows sufficiency under assumed parameters; the claim does not present it as evidence that SES did produce the pattern.
claims.note: Checked: no causal effect of cannabis in the model; 500 runs; trend test significant at 5% in about 50% of runs (also about 60% at 10% and about 30% at 1%). 'The main pattern' is right: what was simulated is the main table of IQ change by waves of dependence. The age-of-onset contrast was not simulated; Rogeberg lists it among the analyses that would separate the two models. Worth adding if space allows: the model assumes its key parameters, notably a temporary schooling boost for lower-SES children of about 4 IQ points (about 0.25 SD) that fades with age, and the paper reports no test of them on Dunedin data. Its one empirical pointer is Meier's own education subgroup: the 3+ group lost 0.45 SD relative to never-users with high school or less (n = 26) against about 0.24 SD with more education (n = 12). Rogeberg's 'n = 35' for the more-educated 2-wave group should be 15 (Meier Table 4: 35 − 20); my recomputation from Meier Table 4 gives 0.45, 0.24, 0.22 and 0.14. Rogeberg gives Meier's sample as 894 against 874 in Meier's Table 1, says childhood IQ was tested at 7, 9 and 11 (Meier: also 13), and says Meier adjusted only for sex and examined confounders one at a time. That last point overlooks Meier's education-adjusted model and the one multivariable model (t = −2.20). Also: the article gives significance rates only at 10%, 5% and 1%, while Meier's trend reached P < 0.0001 (t = −4.45); how often the no-effect model produced a result that strong is not reported.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of direction or size, but two qualifiers are missing. (1) Exposure: 'daily use' here is the frequency of the person's most consistent lifetime pattern of use (Methods > Measures, 2nd paragraph), not current use; current use was not associated after full adjustment (1.1, 0.9-1.5, p = 0.36; Table 2). Suggest 'daily use as the most consistent pattern over the lifetime'. (2) Comparator: the 1.6 (1.1-2.1) for first use at 15 or younger is against people who never used (Table 2 footnote), which the claim does not say; against that reference it is close to the ever-use estimate of 1.3. 'Develop' is acceptable for incident first-episode cases, though the estimates are odds of case status in a case-control design.
claims.note: Checked against Table 2 and the Results text, all matching: 901 cases and 1,237 controls at 11 sites (London, Cambridge, Amsterdam, Gouda and Voorhout, Paris Val-de-Marne, Puy de Dome, Madrid, Barcelona, Bologna, Palermo, Ribeirao Preto); daily use 3.2 (2.2-4.1) against never or occasional use; more than once a week 1.4 (1.0-2.0), p = 0.066; ever use 1.3 (1.1-1.6); first use at 15 or younger 1.6 (1.1-2.1); daily use 3.1 (2.1-5.2) after adding age at first use; adjustment set as stated (Table 2 footnote). Daily use was reported by 29.5% of cases and 6.8% of controls, supporting 'reported more often'. The comparator for daily use is printed two ways: Table 2's reference row is never or occasional use, while the Summary, Results 7th paragraph and Discussion 1st paragraph say never users; the claim follows the table, the more cautious reading. Alcohol: Methods > Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph lists drinks per day among the confounders, but alcohol did not differ between groups (Results, 5th paragraph, p = 0.45) and is absent from the adjustment footnotes of Table 2 and Figure 1, so the 2019 models appear not to include it, which fits the claim's 'adjusted also for alcohol' for the 2015 study. The occasional-use ORs 0.84 (low potency) and 0.96 (high potency) are not in the text; Figure 1 (viewed 2026-10-31, after the card check) shows them as 'rare use', with error bars spanning 1: confirmed. Controls were quota-sampled from address and GP lists and topped up through advertisements and leaflets for hard-to-reach groups, then weighted to census age, gender and ethnicity (Methods > Participants, 2nd paragraph; Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph): 'population controls' is the source's own term but includes some advertisement recruitment.

claims.overstatement: Slight, on framing: the claim says the reviews give absolute figures only as calculations that assume the association is causal. Hall (2015) presents 7 rising to 14 in 1,000 as its best estimate of risk in people who do not use and in people who use regularly, without stating a causal condition for that sentence (the explicit causal assumption introduces the next sentence). Applying a doubling to a base rate does treat the association as the effect, so the claim's reading is defensible, but 'given as the review's best estimate, by applying a doubling to a base rate' would be closer.
claims.note: The base rate (7 in 1,000) is cited to a systematic review of the prevalence of schizophrenia (ref 102, Saha et al., 2005), applied to people who do not use cannabis and called the risk of developing a psychosis. Two further absolute illustrations on the same page are explicitly conditional and not in the claim: about 4,700 young men aged 20-24 in the UK would have to be dissuaded to prevent one case, if causal (ref 99); and a rise from 10% to 20% for people with an affected first-degree relative who use regularly, if risks are independent and multiplicative (ref 103). The review also supports the claim's core with Moore et al.'s pooled 1.4 (1.20-1.65) and 2.09 (1.54-2.84) and the Swedish conscript gradient. Its conclusions assert that the doubling is greater with a personal or family history and with first use in the mid-teens, without data in the body for the age effect; the claim's 'not shown' stands, but the editors may wish to note that this review asserts it.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of Marconi's result; three precision points. (1) 'Against never use': the Methods say never users were always the reference, but Table 1's reference rows read 'No cannabis within last year' (Wiles), 'None' or 'No use' for frequency of use at baseline (Henquet, Degenhardt) and 'No cannabis use at age 18' (Arseneault); 'against no use (never, or none in the period each study measured)' would match the table. (2) 3.90 is the fitted odds ratio at the very top of the ranking (x = 1, the single heaviest-ranked person in each study), not the odds for a top category as a group; the paper gives 3.40 (2.55-4.54) for the median person in the top 20% and 1.97 (1.68-2.31) for the median person who used at all, and says its estimate is for the most severe user, not the average user in the top category. (3) Understatement: 'no source read gives absolute risks by level of use' is not quite true of this source. Table 1 prints cases and totals at every level, so crude absolute risks can be read off for the six cohorts (editors' calculation, unadjusted; follow-up lengths are not given here): Swedish conscripts, admission for schizophrenia, 215 of 36,429 (0.59%) with no use vs 28 of 731 (3.8%) with more than 50 occasions; Dunedin, schizophreniform disorder at 26, 12 of 494 (2.4%) vs 3 of 29 (10.3%).
claims.note: Every number from this source checked and matching: 10 studies, 66,816 people (Table 1 rows sum to 66,816, editors' calculation); pooled b 1.36 (1.04-1.68), OR 3.90 (2.84-5.34), I2 82%; crude counts with nothing adjusted (Methods > Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph). Recomputed: all 38 crude category ORs in Table 1 reproduce from their counts within 0.006; exp(1.36) = 3.90, exp(0.5 x 1.36) = 1.97 and exp(0.9 x 1.36) = 3.40 as printed. A DerSimonian-Laird pooling of the ten per-study estimates read from Figure 3 gives 3.90 (2.84-5.35), I2 81.7%, reproducing the printed result, as do the subgroup totals. 'Category-level odds that did not rise steadily in several studies' is right: by Table 1, 6 of 10 studies have at least one exposed category below a lower one or below 1 (Tien 0.84 at moderate use; Swedish conscripts 0.56 and 0.98 at 1 and 2-4 occasions; Henquet 4.89 then 3.96; Miettunen 3.32 then 3.00; ALSPAC 3.11 then 1.42; GAP 0.70, 0.40, 0.65 before 1.24 and 3.51). The fitted curves of Figure 2, on which the authors base 'a consistent increase ... in all the included studies', are rising by construction (one log-linear slope per study). The exposure scales differ between studies: lifetime frequency, past-year frequency, duration of use, dependence, and in Dunedin age at first use (use by 15 ranked above use by 18). The diagnosis subgroup (5.07, 3.62-7.09) contains two studies only (Swedish conscripts and GAP); Arseneault's schizophreniform disorder is pooled with the symptom studies in Figure 3B, although Table 1 and the Results list it as a diagnosis. One of the ten datasets (GAP) is the authors' own, replaced with new data they supplied (Figure 1; Results, 1st paragraph). The authors write that a causal link cannot be unequivocally established (Discussion, 8th paragraph), while the abstract says high levels of use increase the risk; the claim's association wording ('found the odds ... rising') matches the evidence. Overlap: five of the six cohorts pooled here were published by 2006 (Tien 1990, Arseneault 2002, Zammit 2002, Henquet 2005, Wiles 2006) and are probably also among Moore et al.'s seven cohorts, so the two reviews are not independent replications (to be checked against Moore's list).

claims.overstatement: (1) The opening 'mainly using low-potency cannabis was not associated with psychosis' holds for low-potency use over all frequencies (1.1, 0.9-1.5), but in this source daily use of low-potency types was associated (2.2, 1.4-3.6), and the authors stress that the dose-response reflects daily use of traditional-strength types as well (Discussion, 2nd paragraph); the claim gives 2.19 later, but the opening sentence reads as if low-potency use carried no association at any frequency. (2) 'Most of all daily' fits the point estimates, but the source found no interaction between frequency and type (p = 0.25) and the two daily intervals overlap (2.5-6.3 and 1.4-3.6), so a larger risk for daily high-potency than daily low-potency use is not statistically shown. (3) 'Mainly' is not in the 2019 main text: Table 2 puts each person who ever used into one potency class (331 + 240 = 571 of 574 controls, 3 missing; 251 + 334 = 585 cases), but how people who used both types were classed is described only in the appendix (not read). (4) Potency was assigned from Europe-wide (EMCDDA 2016) as well as national data on expected THC by type, not from national means alone.
claims.note: Checked and matching: 901 cases, 1,237 controls, 11 sites in the UK, Netherlands, France, Spain, Italy and Brazil, May 2010 to April 2015; high-potency use in 37.1% of cases and 19.4% of controls (Table 2; Table 3 prints 35.1% and 19.1% for the same exposure in the whole sample); fully adjusted ORs against never use 1.6 (1.2-2.2) high, 1.1 (0.9-1.5) low; 1.5 (1.1-2.6) for high potency after controlling for daily use; daily high potency 4.8 (2.5-6.3) and daily low potency 2.2 (1.4-3.6) in the text (the claim's 4.78 and 2.19 round to these); site ORs for high potency 0.6 (Palermo) to 3.6 (Amsterdam), variation by site p = 0.45; attributable fraction 12.2% (3.0-16.1) assuming causality (Summary and Table 3; Results, 12th paragraph misprints the interval as 3.0-6.1). Editors' recomputation by Miettinen's formula (case prevalence x (OR - 1) / OR): 13.2% with Table 3's 35.1% (13.9% with Table 2's 37.1%) against the printed model-based 12.2%; daily use 20.3% against 20.4%; London high potency 30.0% against 30.3%; Amsterdam 50.3% as printed. 4.78, 2.19, the more-than-weekly 1.57 and 1.36 and the occasional 0.96 and 0.84 come only from Figure 1: confirmed there (viewed 2026-10-31, after the card check). The 2019 paper calls the 2015 study its previous finding (reference 28) and cites its 24% figure, confirming the shared team; the London site's catchment is not named in the 2019 main text. Several printed 95% intervals are strongly asymmetric on the log scale (daily high potency 4.8, 2.5-6.3; whole-sample daily 3.2, 2.2-4.1; London daily 3.6, 1.4-4.4; Madrid daily 2.5, 2.1-7.3), which Wald intervals from a logistic model would not produce; the method for the intervals is not stated.

claims.overstatement: Slight, for the polygenic-score sentence. The review says only that Di Forti et al. examined schizophrenia polygenic scores in people using low- and high-potency cannabis and found no evidence that high-potency users were more genetically predisposed; it gives no sample size or figures, and its reference 90 is the authors' reply in Lancet Psychiatry correspondence (2015;2:382), not a peer-reviewed report. 'Did not differ' asserts a null result that the review does not show; suggested wording: 'reported finding no evidence that schizophrenia polygenic scores were higher in people using high-potency cannabis (from the team's own correspondence reply; no figures given)'.
claims.note: Murray's description of the 2015 south London study gives 410 first-episode patients and 390 healthy controls, while the claim gives 370 controls, so the control count should be checked at Di Forti et al. (2015) itself, which I could not read (check page at the publisher). Murray summarizes that study as daily high-potency use carrying five times the odds and hashish use no increased risk, and suggests the latter may reflect hashish's lower THC and its cannabidiol, a speculation, since cannabidiol was not measured. In its Conclusions, Murray gives the share of psychosis that could be prevented if nobody used cannabis as 8% to 24%, citing only the 2015 study; per Di Forti et al. (2019, Research in context panel) the 24% is that study's figure for high-potency use, so Murray's framing mislabels it as a fraction for all cannabis use, and states no causal assumption. THC figures in the review (rise from 3% or less in the 1960s; about 16% in England and 20% in the Netherlands in the early 2000s; high-THC plants with only traces of cannabidiol) are second-hand.

claims.overstatement: None with respect to this source. The claim attributes no figure to it; the design (first-episode case-control study plus a cross-site ecological correlation) cannot show causation, and the source's own attributable fractions are computed on the assumption of causality, which fits 'evidence is insufficient'.
claims.note: Qualifying role only. Editors' calculation from Table 2 (excess odds removed = (crude OR - adjusted OR) / (crude OR - 1)): daily use 58%, high potency 73%, ever use 79%, first use at 15 or younger 79%, low potency 90%, current use 94%. The 'crude' ORs are already weighted and adjusted for age, gender and ethnicity, so this measures only the further adjustment for education, employment, tobacco and other drugs; it is not comparable with the 45% (Moore et al., 2007), which starts from unadjusted estimates. The authors read their results causally (Research in context panel; Discussion, 12th paragraph) while stating that the attributable fractions assume causality (Methods, Statistical analysis, 4th paragraph). The selection-bias analysis (Results, 14th paragraph) addresses selection only, and its 'original' daily-use OR of 5.7 (4.4-7.5) matches no OR in Table 2.

claims.overstatement: None for the figures attributed to this source: each matches the source with the right unit (per doubling of the odds of ever use), the right exposure (genetic liability to ever use, ICC ever/never phenotype) and the right outcome (schizophrenia case status, PGC2). Two omissions, not overstatements: (1) the claim does not say that none of the 21 variants reached genome-wide significance (all at p < 10^-5; the authors say some may be false positives); (2) the authors' own reading (some evidence of a small causal effect of initiation; at most a 24% higher relative risk at the upper confidence bound for 50% vs 10% probability of initiation; stronger evidence for the reverse direction) is not given, although the claim gives the narrative reviews' readings. 'Pleiotropy-robust' for MR-Egger is acceptable; the source calls it 'more robust to pleiotropy' (valid under its own assumption).
claims.note: Gage's 'where this is reported' instrument strength: the paper gives no F statistic and no variance explained by the 21 SNPs; the 13-20% in the Method is the SNP-based variance explained by the whole-genome GWAS of ever use, not the instrument, and must not be used as instrument strength. Sensitivity analyses for other pathways: MR-Egger (intercept OR 0.99, 0.98-1.01, p = 0.50), 12-SNP restriction, leave-one-out (supplement only), positive control education (weak, 0.99, 0.97-1.00, p = 0.066) and negative control height (null, 1.00, 0.99-1.01). Reverse-direction MR-Egger 1.17 (0.96-1.43), p = 0.13, is not in the claim and is the one figure that weakens the reverse-direction result the claim cites. Units: 1.04 per doubling corresponds to about 1.06 per unit of log odds (editors' conversion check: exp(ln 1.04 / 0.693) = 1.058), close to Vaucher's 1.08 per unit; the claim keeps the units apart correctly, but a reader comparing 1.04 with 1.08 may think the second is twice as large. Recomputed the authors' 24% upper bound: exp((logit 0.5 - logit 0.1) x ln(1.07)/0.693) = 1.239, same; the formula as printed in Method > Sensitivity analyses, 5th paragraph (log(UCB/0.693)) would give 2.60, so the printed formula has a misplaced bracket. 'These three studies share consortium data': for this source, exposure data are the ICC GWAS (Stringer et al. 2016) and outcome data PGC2 (2014), with an EGCUT overlap of about 1,500 people between the two; supported.

claims.overstatement: None. If anything the claim understates Murray's position slightly: Murray calls cannabis a component (contributory) cause and says the evidence is sufficient for public-health messages about the risk, especially of regular high-potency and synthetic-cannabinoid use; 'strong enough for a public-health message that cannabis can increase the risk' is Gage et al.'s phrase, which Murray quotes and adopts. The claim's grouping is fair as a description of how this review reads the evidence.
claims.note: Murray is from the same group as several studies it relies on (the south London case-control studies; its last author is Di Forti), and it rebuts the sceptical readings (Ksir & Hart, 2016; Hill, 2015; Haney & Evins, 2016) without new data. It reports no Mendelian randomization or co-relative study. Its genetic discussion describes schizophrenia polygenic risk as explaining only a very small share of cannabis use (Power et al., 2014, second-hand), which is in the same direction as the claim's 'genetic liability to schizophrenia making cannabis use more likely', but Murray treats it as minor. The Andreasson et al. (1987) figure, six times the risk with more than 50 occasions over 15 years in 45,750 conscripts, is given without saying whether it is adjusted; from general knowledge, not from this source, six is the unadjusted relative risk, which fell to about 2.3 after adjustment in the original paper, an example of the attenuation the claim describes (to be checked at the original if used). Table 1's adjusted odds ratios for 13 longitudinal analyses range from 1.1 (0.76-1.65) to 4.5 (1.1-18.2); the Henquet entry is printed 1.7 (1.1-1.5), an interval that excludes its own estimate.

claims.overstatement: None for the figures attributed to this source. Every Pasman figure in the statement and magnitude matches, with the right exposure (genetic liability to lifetime ever use; instruments of 5 genome-wide significant SNPs and of 69 SNPs at p < 10^-5), outcome (schizophrenia, PGC 2014) and adjustment (none beyond the GWAS covariates). Points for the editor: (1) the forward Pasman estimates are given without a unit in the statement and magnitude; they are on the same per-unit-of-log-odds scale as the reverse estimate and Vaucher's 1.08, and the claim should say so. (2) The claim's 'per unit of log odds' is the correct reading but is not the source's own label: Table 3's footnote describes the odds ratios as the odds for lifetime users vs non-users (forward) and for people with vs without a schizophrenia diagnosis (reverse), a description the Author Correction undercuts for the reverse direction (few participants in the cannabis GWAS have a diagnosis; the exposure is liability). The claim should keep its own label and note that the source labels the scale differently. (3) The 69-SNP instrument is below genome-wide significance (p < 10^-5); the claim implies but does not state this. (4) For the reverse direction the claim gives the IVW estimate only; MR-Egger SIMEX was null (1.07, p = 0.81), which the authors attribute to low power. Not an overstatement, because the claim words the reverse result as an association.
claims.note: Recomputed from Table 3 (B, SE): forward 69 SNPs exp(0.091 +/- 1.96 x 0.051) = 1.10 (0.99-1.21), p = 0.074; forward 5 SNPs 1.04 (0.76-1.42), p = 0.805 (printed 0.806; the claim's 0.81 is right); GSMR 74 SNPs exp(0.192) = 1.21 (1.04-1.42), p = 0.016 (printed 0.017); reverse exp(0.151 +/- 1.96 x 0.046) = 1.16 (1.06-1.27), p = 0.001. Same as the claim. Instrument strength (Discussion, 7th paragraph): the cannabis instruments explained 1.12% (69 SNPs) and 0.15% (5 SNPs) of variance in ever use, which matches 'about 1% or less' (1.12% counts as about 1%); the schizophrenia instrument explained 3.38% of liability variance. No F statistic is reported. Editors' F from these figures: about 30 (69 SNPs), 54 (5 SNPs) and 42 (schizophrenia). The variance figures are approximations (Online Methods > Causal association..., 6th paragraph: one SNP's p-value sets the phenotypic variance) using effective sample sizes (130,072 schizophrenia; 180,934 cannabis) that I could not reproduce from the counts in the paper with the stated formula (editors' calculation from the reported prevalences of use: about 151,500 for cannabis; PGC2 with 36,989 cases and 113,075 controls gives about 111,500). The variance explained may therefore be somewhat larger than printed, but stays about 1%. Shared data: exposure GWAS = ICC (35,297; the same consortium that supplied Gage's and Vaucher's instruments) + 23andMe + UK Biobank; outcome = PGC 2014 schizophrenia GWAS, as in Gage. The paper reports no check of sample overlap, which supports 'not independent'. The task file's title is the corrected title; the PMC manuscript carries the original 'a causal influence of schizophrenia'.

claims.overstatement: None for the figures attributed to this source: 1.08 (1.02-1.14) per unit of log odds of ever use, the authors' rescaling to 1.37 (1.09-1.67) users vs non-users, and 1.41 (1.09-1.83) from the multivariable MR adjusted for the variants' associations with ever smoking all match, with the right exposure (genetic liability to ever use; ICC 10 lead SNPs) and outcome (schizophrenia, PGC). The claim rightly attributes the rescaling to the authors; it is not an editors' calculation. Omissions: the 10 variants did not reach genome-wide significance (p 4.6 x 10^-7 to 3.1 x 10^-6), and the authors' own reading (the genetic approach 'strongly supports' a causal relation) is not reported, although the claim reports the narrative reviews' readings; the claim's headline ('evidence is insufficient') is the editors' synthesis, which this source's authors do not share, and status 'contested' covers this only if the authors' view is named.
claims.note: Instrument strength: the 10 SNPs explain 1% of variance in ever use (Results), matching 'about 1% or less'; F statistics only in the supplement; the authors report I2 = 67% for MR-Egger (potential relative bias 43%) and therefore applied simulation extrapolation (results only in Supplementary Table S7). Sensitivity analyses for other pathways: MR-Egger gave no evidence of directional pleiotropy (p = 0.292; its estimate is not given in the main text), weighted median similar but less precise (no number in the main text), leave-one-out largely unchanged, no outlier SNP, two SNPs with marginal influence; two putatively functional SNPs (KCNT2, NCAM1) gave 1.88 (1.00-3.21); the authors concede MR-Egger and weighted median may be underpowered. The rescaling from 1.08 per unit to 1.37 users vs non-users uses schizophrenia risk in the population and its prevalence in people who never used cannabis, described only in the supplement, so it cannot be checked from the main text; by my arithmetic it corresponds to a contrast of about 4.1 units of log odds of ever use (ln 1.37 / ln 1.08), a large extrapolation from a 1%-variance instrument. On the comparable scale, 1.08 per unit is about 1.055 per doubling of the odds, close to Gage et al. 2017's 1.04. Shared data: ICC (Stringer et al. 2016, 32,330 people) for exposure and the public PGC schizophrenia GWAS (34,241 cases, 45,604 controls) for outcome, the same consortia as Gage et al. 2017; overlap between exposure and outcome data under 5%. Supports 'not independent'. Locators of my anchors were refined after step 2 to name the printed sub-subheadings under 'Characteristics of the genetic markers'; places and data unchanged.

claims.overstatement: The claim's 'ecological correlation' is the right description; the source's own wording overstates (it presents the cross-site correlation as the first direct evidence that cannabis use affects variation in incidence). Not supported as worded: 'two strongly overlapping measures' (see note).
claims.note: Supported: incidence adjusted for age, gender and ethnicity correlated with the prevalence of daily use among controls (r = 0.8, p = 0.0109) and of high-potency use (r = 0.7, p = 0.0286); 10 sites, because Figure 3 omits Puy-de-Dome (no adjusted rate), although the Summary and Results 16th paragraph say 11. The printed p-values fit 10 sites: with 8 degrees of freedom they correspond to r of about 0.76 and 0.69, whereas r = 0.8 at 11 sites would give p of about 0.003. Not supported as worded: the source states that the two prevalences were only modestly correlated (r = 0.2, p = 0.0413; Results, 16th paragraph). That printed pair cannot hold at 10-11 sites (r = 0.2 gives p of about 0.56-0.58; p = 0.041 needs about 100 observations). The editors' recomputation from the site prevalences in Table 3 gives r = 0.71 (10 sites, p about 0.02) or 0.73 (11 sites, p about 0.011), which agrees with the claim's description. The claim should label the overlap an editors' calculation from Table 3 and mention the printed r = 0.2, or drop it. Minor: Bologna's daily-use prevalence is 3 of 65 controls (4.6%) in the text but 4.1% in Table 3. Figure 3 (viewed 2026-10-31, after the card check) gives the same picture: from the plotted points, daily use and high-potency use among controls correlate at r of about 0.71-0.76.

Supported: Gage gives three of the reasons the claim attributes jointly to Gage and Hall (individuals' use and illness not linked, i.e. the ecological fallacy; confounders not accounted for; other competing risk factors that may have declined). Not in Gage: that even a causal effect would raise incidence only modestly, and that changing diagnostic criteria, services and records could hide or create trends; these must rest on Hall (2015). Contradicted in part: the claim says the British general-practice study is 'known only through a 2008 government advisory report' (magnitude: 'third-hand'), but Gage cites it directly as a published paper: ref. 61, Frisher et al. (2009), Schizophrenia Research, on trends in diagnosed schizophrenia in the UK from 1996 to 2005, among studies finding 'no change, or a decrease'. Also for the editor: two of Gage's four citations in this paragraph do not match their statements by title (ref. 58, Ajdacic-Gross et al., 2009, is on adult versus adolescent onset of smoking; ref. 60, Breslau et al., 2006, on race-ethnic differences in psychiatric disorder); ref. 59 (Boydell et al., 2003) covers south-east London 1965-1997.

claims.overstatement: Mild: Moore does not make the time-lag point on its own data; it reports what 'other projections' suggest, citing ref. 61 (Hickman et al., 2007, model projections for England and Wales), which is probably the same British modelling study the claim already lists ('too early to see any rise in England and Wales'). 'The 2007 systematic review adds' presents a citation as the review's own contribution and may make one modelling study look like two sources.
claims.note: The same paragraph also reports that projected schizophrenia trends have not paralleled cannabis trends and that this mismatch has been used as an argument against causation (ref. 60, Degenhardt, Hall & Lynskey, 2003, the Australian modelling study), consistent with the claim's 'studies disagree'. Second-hand throughout, as the claim says.

claims.overstatement: None for the part Murray supports. Attribution precision: the claim cites Murray together with Hall & Degenhardt (2009) and Hall (2015) after a list of five studies, but Murray describes only the south-east London study (and the sceptics' argument in general terms); the Australian and English modelling studies, Zurich and the general-practice study are not in Murray.
claims.note: Murray supports the south-east London part: incidence of schizophrenia described as doubling between 1965 and 1999, with the share of patients with schizophrenia who used cannabis rising more than among other psychiatric patients (Boydell et al., 2006, ref 85; the location comes from the reference title). Murray calls it the only competent study spanning several decades with constant research criteria, and uses it against the sceptical argument that incidence did not change while use rose; it also says reliable information on trends in incidence is scarce, which supports 'evidence is insufficient'. Murray does not mention the ecological nature of the comparison. No numbers beyond 'doubled' and the dates.

claims.overstatement: None. One small inexactness: 'in the same survey' does not quite hold for tobacco; the 31.9% divides NCS tobacco dependence, assessed in a 55% subsample (4,414) and asking only about daily smoking, by tobacco-use prevalence from the 1991 NHSDA, which is why it has no standard error (pp. 248, 251). The magnitude's '(no SE)' is right.
claims.note: All Anthony numbers confirmed on the page images: 8,098; 82.4%; 46.3% (SE 1.1); 4.2% (0.3); 9.1% (0.7); tobacco 31.9% (no SE), heroin 23.1% (5.6), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), alcohol 15.4% (0.7) (Table 2, p. 251); men 12.0% (1.1), women 5.5% (0.7) (Table 5, p. 259; also p. 264). Recomputed: 4.2/46.3 = 9.07%; 9.1 +/- 1.96 x 0.7 = 7.7 to 10.5, as the claim's editors' calculation says; 6.2/51.7 = 12.0% and 2.3/41.0 = 5.6% (printed 5.5, rounding of unrounded inputs). Use was counted from a single occasion, so 'even once' is right (p. 248). The limitations sentence matches the source: dependence assessed only after several occasions of use (p. 248); 15-24-year-olds had just entered the main risk period (p. 262) with many years at risk left (p. 264); incomplete reporting of dependence problems would attenuate the proportion dependent among users (p. 263); deaths give an undercount and forgotten or casual use an overcount (p. 264). Not in the claim: the authors say overall rates change little when institutional residents are included, though perhaps not for groups with high incarceration (p. 265); and the earlier ECA survey gave close to 20% DSM-III abuse or dependence among people who had used cannabis more than five times (p. 263), which shows how much the figure depends on the denominator.

claims.overstatement: Not an overstatement but an incomplete description of how this review uses 'about 1 in 10'. The claim says the reviews' 'about 9 in 100, or about 1 in 10' is cited to the US surveys or matches them, and for Connor names the 1990-92 survey. That is true of the 9% in Epidemiology > Prevalence. But Connor's abstract says the use disorder affects about 10% of the 193 million people worldwide who use cannabis, and its introduction says it occurs in about 1 in 10 'regular users'. Both cite the UN World Drug Report and use denominators (people who used in the past year worldwide; regular users) that do not match the surveys' denominator (anyone who had ever used).
claims.note: Supported parts: the 9% and its comparison figures (tobacco 32%, heroin 23%, cocaine 17%, alcohol 15%), cited to ref. 30 (Anthony, Warner & Kessler 1994, the NCS). Connor dates the estimate 'in 1992'; the fieldwork ran 1990-92 and the paper appeared in 1994. DSM-5 use disorder needs 2 of 11 criteria with marked clinical impairment or distress over 12 months, with severity graded mild (2-3), moderate (4-5) and severe (6+). About 30% of people who use cannabis may develop a use disorder in recent US national data, cited to Hasin et al. 2015 (ref. 32); Connor gives neither the measure nor the denominator (it does not say past-year use) and suggests the rise may reflect potency, legal status and acceptance. 'Narrower' (DSM-III-R and DSM-IV dependence against DSM-5 use disorder) is the editors' inference. Connor supports it: DSM-5 merged abuse and dependence on evidence of a single severity dimension, and Table 1 marks 7 of the 11 DSM-5 criteria as DSM-IV-TR dependence criteria. Connor does not state the DSM-IV threshold. Internal inconsistency: 193 million (abstract) against 192 million (introduction and Prevalence) people using in the past year.

claims.overstatement: None.
claims.note: Curran's 8.9% (cocaine 20.9%, alcohol 22.7%, tobacco 67.5%) is cited to ref 64, Lopez-Quintero et al. (2011, NESARC), as the claim says; Curran calls DSM-IV dependence 'becoming addicted' and gives no interval. Box 3 supports the claim's description of DSM-5 cannabis use disorder (2 or more symptoms within 12 months, mild with 2-3; eleven criteria counting the seven DSM-IV dependence items, three of the four abuse items and craving), which the claim cites to Connor et al. (2021).

claims.overstatement: Two small wording points. (1) 'With a median of about 5 years from first use to dependence': the source says half of the cases of cannabis dependence were observed about 5 years after first use, i.e. a median among those who became dependent, not among everyone who used. (2) The lead sentence says about 9 in 100 'had at some point met criteria'; that fits the NCS figure, but the NESARC 8.9% is a life-table projection of how many would become dependent at some time in life (the body of the claim words it correctly).
claims.note: All numbers confirmed: 7,389 cannabis users (abstract; Methods 2.1); 8.9%, 5.9% at a decade, 'almost 2.0%' after the first year (given jointly for nicotine, alcohol and cannabis), 67.5%, 22.7%, 20.9%, and half of cannabis cases about 5 years after first use (Results 3.3). The cumulative figures are projections from the standard actuarial method, with no intervals in the text or in Figure 1. Wave 2 is dated 2004-2005 in the text; the Wave 1 dates (2001-2002) appear only in a reference title. The sample is the 34,653 Wave 1 respondents re-interviewed at Wave 2 (of 43,093), so people who died between waves (1,403) are not included; Wave 2 response is not stated (editors' calculation: about 87% of the eligible). Not in the claim: the lifetime projection varied by racial-ethnic group from 8.2% (White) to 15.9% (Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander), log-rank 17.57, p < 0.01; and the paper calls its 5.9% at a decade consistent with the NCS estimate it cites as 8% (Wagner & Anthony, 2002). Reporting inconsistencies: the cannabis subgroup counts in Tables 1 and 2 sum to 7,409, not 7,389; Table 2 counts 564 users with lifetime cannabis dependence while Tables 3-4 give N = 529.

claims.overstatement: None.
claims.note: Volkow cites the about-9% figure to the NESARC analysis (ref 3, Lopez-Quintero et al. 2011), as the claim says, and phrases it as a lifetime projection (people who experiment 'will become addicted'), matching NESARC's cumulative probability. The same paragraph gives NSDUH 2012 counts (2.7 million with DSM-IV marijuana dependence), which the claim does not use.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim correctly says the age groups are by age at interview, not age at first use, and attributes the before-17 point to studies the authors cite.
claims.note: Table 4 figures confirmed on the page image (p. 256): dependence among people who had used cannabis 15.3% (SE 2.3) at 15-24, 8.1% (0.7) at 25-34, 8.5% (1.3) at 35-44 and 3.1% (1.5) at 45-54 (labelled 45+ in a sample aged 15-54). Recomputed from the same rows: 5.6/36.5 = 15.3%, 5.0/61.6 = 8.1%, 4.4/52.1 = 8.4% (printed 8.5), 0.8/25.5 = 3.1%. The authors' own reading (p. 264): 15-24-year-olds had a comparatively high proportion dependent although they had many years at risk left, possibly because early-onset users (before 17) seem at higher risk of drug problems even after adjustment for duration of use (Anthony & Petronis, 1993; Robins & Przybeck, 1985), so the figure may fall as later starters join. Not in the claim: the authors also suggest that age differences may reflect birth cohort, period and drug availability, and that drug-related deaths deplete older groups (p. 261), which bear on the low 3.1% at 45-54 as much as on the high figure at 15-24.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim softens Connor's causal wording ('initiation before 16 years of age increases the risk') to 'linked to', which is appropriate for second-hand observational figures. The claim correctly flags Connor's arithmetic: 9.7% is about 1 in 10.3, while 'almost 1 in 19' would be about 5.3% (recomputed).
claims.note: All the figures attributed to Connor are found, with the citations the claim names: ref 45 is Cougle et al. 2016 (J Clin Psychiatry; NESARC, concurrent and prospective analyses of regular users); refs 15 and 31 are the 'two reviews' for 30-40% (Budney, Sofis & Borodovsky 2019, a review with policy commentary; Coffey & Patton 2016, a review of findings from one Australian cohort, the Victorian Adolescent Health Cohort Study); ref 1 is the UN World Drug Report 2020 for 'as many as one-third' of daily users; refs 39-41 are the three sources for first use before 16 (Butterworth et al., 2007 Australian national survey; Le Strat et al. 2015, US; Behrendt et al. 2009); refs 37, 42 and 43 support early onset (a book chapter, a genetics review, a twin meta-analysis). Connor gives no definitions, measures or adjustment for any of these figures. Omission in the claim: the same sentence that gives one-third for daily use also gives 'approximately 1 in 10 regular users' (UN report), a frequency figure on yet another denominator. Consistent with the claim: Connor lists negative life events as independent predictors of incident use disorder, citing van der Pol et al. 2013; and it calls the lack of measures of THC consumed a major limitation of epidemiological research, where only frequency is usually assessed.

claims.overstatement: None. One description differs from Curran's text: Curran describes the 3-year study's sample as 'daily users' (p. 301), while the claim says 'people who used frequently', which matches the title of Curran's ref 215 (van der Pol et al., 2013, 'transition from frequent cannabis use to cannabis dependence'). Probably right for the primary study, but the claim attributes the description to Curran.
claims.note: Curran's text: variables directly related to cannabis use did not predict transition to 'addiction' (the study's outcome was dependence, by its title); living alone, coping motives and negative life events (such as a major financial crisis) were 'more important'. The same subsection names early adolescent onset and frequent (especially daily) use as risk factors, citing two studies (Coffey et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2005), with concurrent tobacco use (three studies), and gives European treatment data (mean age at first treatment 24, at first use 16; 83% male). Box 3 (p. 299) lists the DSM-IV dependence criteria, including use in larger amounts or over a longer period than intended and a great deal of time spent obtaining, using or recovering, which supports the editors' remark that frequent use is partly built into the criteria.

claims.overstatement: None material. Two precision points: (1) 'stepwise adjustment for sociodemographic factors, psychiatric disorders and dependence on other substances' describes a model chosen by stepwise selection; for cannabis it kept sex, age group at interview and race-ethnicity (no income, education, marital, employment or nativity term), mood, anxiety and personality disorders, and nicotine, alcohol and cocaine dependence; (2) the authors' reading is hedged (transition 'may not be a consequence of early substance use onset per se').
claims.note: Numbers confirmed: before 14 against at or after 14 (Methods 2.3.3; Table 2), unadjusted HR 2.47 (95% CI 2.0-3.1, Table 3), adjusted 0.63 (0.5-0.9, Table 4); in the adjusted cannabis model mood disorder 2.69 (1.9-3.9), anxiety disorder 2.31 (1.6-3.4), personality disorder 2.3 (1.7-3.1), alcohol dependence 2.55 (1.8-3.5), cocaine dependence 4.14 (2.3-7.6), and also nicotine dependence 2.06 (1.4-3.1), male sex 1.44, age 18-29 against 45+ 3.09. Column alignment checked in the page's table HTML. Unweighted, 1,051 cannabis users started before 14 and 6,339 at or after 14. Not in the claim and worth a clause: mood, anxiety and other substance use disorders entered as time-dependent covariates, so the adjusted estimate also conditions on disorders that may follow early use; the reversal therefore does not show that early onset itself protects, which the claim does not say but a reader might infer. The authors also suggest later starters may have more intense use and easier access in late adolescence. The source measured neither frequency of use nor THC.

claims.overstatement: None as to Volkow. The review's own language is causal (the evidence 'clearly indicates' that long-term use can lead to addiction; Table 1 lists addiction as an effect of long-term or heavy use), and the claim rightly keeps to association.
claims.note: All Volkow figures re-found. Precision point: in Volkow the 9% is cited to Lopez-Quintero et al. 2011 (ref 3), while one in six and 25-50% are cited to Hall & Degenhardt 2009 (ref 4); the claim's parenthesis 'Volkow et al., 2014, citing Hall & Degenhardt, with 17% in its table' is right for one in six, but could be read as covering the 9 in 100 as well. Whether ref 4 contains the 25-50% figure cannot be judged from this source (not my source to check). No definition of daily use, no denominators and no adjustment are given with any of the figures, as the claim says. Table 1's footnote asserts, without a citation, that addiction is strongly associated with initial use early in adolescence.

claims.overstatement: None as far as Bahji et al. are concerned: the claim is more cautious than the review, which presents 47% as the prevalence among people with regular or dependent use and says in its Conclusions that withdrawal was more common in men. 'Depended strongly on where the sample came from' describes between-study differences in pooled prevalence, which is how the source reports them; it is not an effect of setting, and the claim does not say it is.
claims.note: Every Bahji number in the statement and magnitude re-found. (1) The population interval 13 to 22 is Table 2's; the abstract and the Results 5th paragraph print 13% to 21%, and Figure 2 prints 0.16 (0.13 to 0.20). (2) The overall 47% (41% to 52%) is the abstract's; the Results 4th paragraph prints 27% to 37%, and Figure 2 prints random effects 0.46 (0.37 to 0.55) and fixed effect 0.28 (0.27 to 0.28). (3) Inpatient n 357 is the text's; Table 1 and Figure 2 give 359. (4) Editors' calculations recomputed: 6,469 of 23,518 = 27.5% (I get 27.51%); Figure 2's event column sums to exactly 6,469, so this is the review's own participant-level count; Table 1 cohort size x prevalence sums to 6,470.0, which is the magnitude's 6,470 (the statement's 6,469 is the abstract's figure; harmonize, both give 27.5%). Unweighted mean of the 50 cohort prevalences in Table 1 = 47.5% (median 49.1%), so 'close to the plain average' holds; the 35 clinical cohorts hold 6,043 of 23,518 participants (25.7%). (5) Only one population cohort used DSM-5 (Livne et al. 2019: 1,527, 12.1%; Figure 2: 185 of 1,527). (6) Bahji's own DSM-5 summary lists 'sleep disturbance' and 'appetite or weight disturbance'; the claim's 'less appetite or weight loss' is the DSM-5 wording, presumably from Connor et al. (2021). The abstract's Importance section places withdrawal on cessation of heavy and prolonged use, a DSM-5 condition the claim's definition leaves out (it says only stopping or cutting down); consider adding it. (7) 'Most predate DSM-5': 46 of the 50 cohorts in Table 1 used DSM-III-R or DSM-IV criteria. (8) The lifetime against past-year contrast, like the tobacco meta-regression, compares studies, not people, and is entangled with setting.

claims.overstatement: The statements attributed to Connor alone, or with Curran, are faithful: the time course, and no serious risk with usually only supportive care when there are no medical or psychiatric comorbidities, which the claim words as 'described as'. The DSM-5 definition, attributed to Bahji and Connor together, differs from Connor's account in two ways. (1) Connor has the signs occurring within 1 week of cessation; it does not mention cutting down, so 'stopping or cutting down' is not supported by this source. (2) Connor includes the requirement that the signs cause clinically severe distress or impairment (Connor's wording), which the claim leaves out. Both widen the definition. The outcome definition counts as an error, not wording, under this round's brief.
claims.note: Connor's time course (begin 24-48 h after cessation, peak within the first week, last 1-2 weeks) is itself second-hand, from Budney et al. 2003 (ref. 176), as the claim's 'second-hand' says. Qualifier for the claim's prevalence figures: Connor repeats Bahji's 17%, 54% and 87% (ref. 203, with Livne 2019, ref. 177) but relabels them. It calls them the prevalence 'in the general population of cannabis users' (12-17%) and the share of treatment-seeking patients with use disorder who report 'clinically severe' withdrawal (54% of outpatients, 87% of inpatients). Connor should not be cited for those figures. Its 12% for frequent users with DSM-5 withdrawal in the past year (Livne 2019) matches the claim's 12.1% from Bahji. Also consistent with the claim: tobacco co-use is linked to more withdrawal symptoms (ref. 46, a systematic review), and CB1 agonists (dronabinol, nabilone, nabiximols) reduced withdrawal intensity. Connor notes that many withdrawal symptoms also occur in other substances' withdrawal and in other mental disorders. In the editors' wording, 'no serious risk' is used only as Connor's statement, with its stated condition; good.

claims.overstatement: Mild. 'THC relieves the symptoms in a dose-dependent way' generalizes Curran's 'can be alleviated by THC in a dose-dependent manner', which rests on one laboratory study of oral THC (ref 73, Budney et al., 2007, by its title). As worded it can read as a suggestion to use more cannabis to ease withdrawal; naming the study condition (oral THC under laboratory conditions) and Curran's note that dronabinol and nabiximols eased withdrawal without reducing use (p. 301) would avoid that.
claims.note: All other Curran attributions recovered on p. 299: around 50% of daily users on stopping, cited to an earlier review (ref 71, Budney et al., 2004); onset 1-2 days, peak 2-6 days, remission 1-2 weeks (the 'one account'); prominent symptoms craving, sleep problems, nightmares, anger, irritability, dysphoria and nausea (ref 72, Allsop et al., 2011); combined cannabis and tobacco withdrawal stronger than either alone in people who use both daily (ref 77, Vandrey et al., 2008, a within-person comparison). Curran also links symptoms to lower CB1 receptor availability in early abstinence.

claims.overstatement: Mild, attribution: the claim says people seeking help to stop 'most often' report anxiety, sleep problems, appetite disturbance and low mood, citing this review. Hall & Degenhardt (2009) lists these among the withdrawal symptoms such people report, without ranking them; the ranking (most common) is in Hall (2015, p. 5), which the claim cites in the next clause. Citing Hall (2015), or both, for that sentence would fix it.
claims.note: Second-hand (ref 40, Budney & Hughes, 2006). The same paragraph notes tolerance in animals and humans, and that a cannabinoid antagonist precipitates a withdrawal syndrome in rats, mice and dogs that THC reverses (animal evidence, ref 39).

claims.overstatement: None in the claim, which does not cite Volkow by name. Volkow's statement that withdrawal makes cessation difficult and contributes to relapse is causal and rests on ref 5, a paper on diagnostic criteria by its title.
claims.note: Volkow is not named in the statement or magnitude; the passage supports the symptom description (irritability, sleep difficulty, dysphoria, craving, anxiety) but gives no prevalence or time course. If the anchor stays, name Volkow et al. (2014) where the symptoms are described, or drop it.

claims.overstatement: None: the claim reports the review's statement as second-hand and gives its two sources.
claims.note: Of the two sources Connor cites for the 90% (refs 189, 190), ref 190 is Sorensen et al. 2017, the claim's own primary source, and ref 189 is a 2019 BMJ clinical review (Chocron, Zuber & Vaucher). Connor's figure therefore adds no independent evidence and should not count towards 'replicated'. Connor's single 90% also merges two features that Sorensen reports separately (relief with hot bathing; relief after stopping). Connor also says almost all patients with the syndrome are heavy weekly users (not in the claim; consistent with Sorensen's weekly-use share) and, in the Quality of life section, that case series suggest heavy smoking 'can result in' the syndrome, a causal wording on case-series evidence. Connor calls it 'cannabis hyperemesis syndrome'.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim describes published cases descriptively, names the absence of comparison groups and of any denominator, and does not present resolution after stopping as proof of cause. It is more cautious than the review, whose Results call the listed features those with the highest sensitivity and whose Discussion speaks of moderate evidence that stopping is the definitive treatment.
claims.note: Every Sorensen number in the statement and magnitude re-found. Recomputed: the review truncates rather than rounds, so 154/211 = 73.0% (printed 72.9%), 157/170 = 92.4% (92.3%), 62/64 = 96.9% (96.8%), 192/197 = 97.5% (97.4%; at least weekly = 50 + 101 + 41 of the 197 with frequency specified), 151/197 = 76.6%, 134/179 = 74.9% (74.8%), 85/211 = 40.3% (40.2%); 45/179 = 25.1%, 65/179 = 36.3%, 30/179 = 16.8%, 39/179 = 21.8% as printed. The claim reproduces the printed values; harmless, but 154 of 211 is 73.0% if the editors prefer their own rounding. Points for the editor: (1) The median ages rest only on the 113 cases with raw data (n = 111, 84 and 101 equal the sums of the Table 1 rows without the 98-patient Simonetto series, which supplied only means), so they do not describe all 211. (2) The 62 of 64 is internally inconsistent in the source: the text attributes the two non-resolving patients to two case reports (Cox et al. 2012; Parikh & Gould 2010), while Table 1 puts one in the Soriano-Co series (4 of 5) and one among the case reports (37 of 38); Table 5 describes a Simonetto patient with no improvement despite self-reported abstinence while Table 1 counts that series as 6 of 6; and Table 1 heads the column 'relief with abstinence or reduction', so 'documented stopping' may include reduction. The claim states what the text says. (3) Return of symptoms on resuming use: Table 2 counts it as too inconsistently documented, as the claim says, but Table 5 relays that in Allen et al.'s series all 3 patients who resumed after a period of abstinence relapsed; the claim could add this. (4) Time to improvement with abstinence was listed for extraction (Data Collection) but never reported, which supports 'no time to resolution is reported'. (5) Frequency categories partly rest on recoding: 'heavy' use was coded as daily and 'frequent' as weekly (Data Analysis), and use was reported in incompatible units (Limitations). (6) On separating CHS from other cyclic vomiting, no study tested the proposed features' accuracy, as the claim says; the closest data are the second-hand cyclic vomiting surveys in Table 4, where hot showers were used by 72% of 31 and 67% of 437 patients with cyclic vomiting syndrome (81% of the latter used cannabis), which bears on how specific hot-bathing relief is.

claims.overstatement: None. 'Links repeated use with increased vomiting without a citation' matches the source, which says only that hyperemesis has been reported with repeated use.
claims.note: The sentence carries no reference number; the review gives no frequency, features or course of the syndrome.

claims.overstatement: Minor. (1) 'In 6 men' (statement and magnitude, twice): the review gives the smoking and urine studies as six subjects (N = 6) and never states their sex; 'mostly involved men' rests on the few studies whose participants the review describes as male (eight males given intravenous THC, 20 male volunteers given tritiated THC, 38 males in the hair study), while Wall et al. dosed women and men. (2) 'Urine stayed positive for up to ... 93 days': the review says only that cannabinoids were detectable for 93 days in that person (no cut-off given); 'positive' applies to the 67-day case (above 20 ng/ml by immunoassay). Otherwise the claim keeps to the source's own framing (association by route and frequency, figures second-hand, single small studies) and does not overstate. Doses appear only as study conditions; the closing sentence about people who feel little at first and take more states an evidence gap, not advice.
claims.note: Every number re-found. Parts supported: all smoked, oral, distribution, half-life, blood and urine figures in the statement and magnitude. Parts not supported by this source: the participants' sex in the 6-person studies, and 'positive' for the 93-day case. Further points: (a) the THC half-life is 'greater than 4.1 d' in 2.4.1 but 'ca. 4.1 d' in 3.1.2 and '4.1 d' in 3.1.4; the claim's 'about 4.1 days' follows 3.1.2 and 3.1.4. (b) The 13-day detection followed four cigarettes containing deuterium-labelled THC, not one labelled dose; the review calls the same protocol deuterium-labelled, isotopically labelled and radiolabelled in different places. (c) The 0.86 ng/ml figure (Peat) is a plasma concentration; the review notes that whole-blood concentrations are about half those in plasma, so the claim's heading 'Blood' should read plasma. (d) The lower-dose cigarette is about 16 mg in 2.1.1, about 15.8 mg in 3.2 and about 18 mg in 2.4.2; the claim's 'about 16 or 34 mg' is the 2.1.1 version. (e) The review states that no pharmacokinetic differences between chronic and occasional users have been substantiated and that terminal half-life did not differ between frequent and infrequent users, so 'frequent use with THC staying in the body for days to weeks' reflects accumulated stores and long detection windows, not slower elimination; the claim could say so. (f) The urine figures of 33.7 and 88.6 hours are mean times of the last positive sample, with negatives interspersed; a naive user's urine may be negative by immunoassay within a few hours of one cigarette.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of the source: the claim says 'is associated with' and states the authors' own caveat on tobacco and alcohol, which is more cautious than the review's abstract (cannabis use may increase adverse outcomes) and Discussion 3rd paragraph (exposure leads to low birth weight). Three small precision points, none changing a number: (1) 'pooled estimates are crude' is the editors' inference; the review states no adjustment (exact), and the mean differences are certainly unadjusted because they were pooled from group means and SDs, but for the odds ratios the review says only that ORs were taken from the papers or computed from their data, without saying whether any OR taken from a paper was adjusted (the forest plots that would show this are in online supplement 4, not read). (2) 'Preterm birth before 37 weeks': the review says 7 of the 8 PTB studies used the WHO <37-week definition (Methods), while the Results and Figure 1 count 9 PTB studies, so the definition was not uniform. (3) 'Tobacco and alcohol, which themselves cause low birth weight and early birth': the source names tobacco and heavy alcohol use (and also small for gestational age). The Apgar, birth-defect and perinatal-death results are narrative vote counts from 2 to 6 studies, not pooled estimates; 'showed no clear difference' is fair wording for that.
