claims.note: Every number from this source re-found: 109.42 g (38.72 to 180.12; rounds to 109, 39 to 180), 10 studies, 4 lower, I2 63%; LBW OR 1.77 (1.04 to 3.01), 7 studies, 2 positive, I2 89%; NICU/ICU OR 2.02 (1.27 to 3.21), 4 studies, 3 positive, I2 78%; PTB OR 1.29 (0.80 to 2.08), 9 studies, I2 85%; gestational age -0.20 (-0.62 to 0.22), 5 studies, fixed effect; length -0.10 (-0.65 to 0.45), I2 59%; head circumference -0.31 (-0.74 to 0.13), I2 97%; anaemia OR 1.36 (1.10 to 1.69), 6 studies, fixed effect. The '6 studies' for length and for head circumference come from Figure 1 (the text says 9 studies reported length and 10 measured head circumference). Editors' count '15 of the 24 articles before 2000' recomputed from the reference list (included refs 13, 16-22, 24-39): before 2000 = refs 13, 20, 22, 24, 25, 27, 28, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38 = 15; 2000 to 2014 = refs 16, 17, 18, 19, 21, 26, 29, 30, 39 = 9; same result. Range 1982 (Greenland) to 2014 (Bonello) confirmed. 'No absolute risks reported' holds for the main text; whether the forest plots in supplement 4 show event counts cannot be judged here. The editors' observation on NICU admission is correct: Discussion 4th paragraph discusses only cost and calls for attention, not whether admission reflects hospital practice toward babies of mothers known to use drugs. The parts citing Hall & Degenhardt 2009, Hall 2015 and Page 2020 are not from this source and were not checked.

claims.overstatement: Mild: the claim relays the review's causal verb (the earlier meta-analysis 'found that regular cannabis smoking in pregnancy reduced birth weight') for a meta-analysis of observational studies. The review uses a causal verb here (decreased) but a hedged one in its conclusions (could reduce); 'was associated with lower birth weight' would be closer to the evidence if the editors avoid relaying causal verbs.
claims.note: Second-hand (refs 29-31: Zuckerman et al. 1989; Fergusson et al. 2002; English et al. 1997, the meta-analysis). The review also lists the confounders that limit interpretation (co-use of tobacco, alcohol and other illicit drugs; less antenatal care; poorer nutrition), which the claim covers in general terms through Gunn et al.'s caveat.

claims.overstatement: None in the statement, which is cautious and matches the AHA's own judgment. The magnitude's Parekh entries 3.12 and 2.63 omit part of the exposure (see note).
claims.note: Supported by Page: the writing group's judgment that the evidence is still inconclusive (e10); 4.8 times baseline in the 60 minutes after use among 3,882 patients, printed without an interval (Table 3, e12), and the 9 patients who had used within the hour (e17); Hemachandra 3.3 (1.8-6.3), 2.3 (1.1-4.5) after adjustment for stroke-related covariates including tobacco, 4.7 (2.1-10.7) with weekly or more frequent use and no elevation with less frequent use (e12); Parekh 1.82 (1.08-3.10), and 2.45 (1.31-4.60) with use on more than 10 days a month, adjustment set not stated (e14; ref 68 is Stroke 2020, so the claim can give the year); Chami & Kim 1.37% vs 0.54%, RR 2.53 (2.45-2.61), adjustment not stated (e11); the selection-bias warning (e10), whose reference list for hospital-based signals includes Chami & Kim; CARDIA (Reis et al. 2017; e12); Frost 29% higher, 95% CI 0.81-2.05, P=0.28 (e11; 'long-term' comes from the reference title); Desai 2019, 0.23% vs 0.14% (e11); Johnson-Sasso OR 0.79 (e12); the listed weaknesses (e9); evidence insufficient especially for people with cardiac risk factors (e17); one cannabis cigarette shortened exercise time to angina by 48% against placebo in people with chronic stable angina (e17; ref 88, a 1974 study). Editors' conversion checked: 1.37% and 0.54% are 13.7 and 5.4 per 1,000 (about 14 and 5); 1.37/0.54 = 2.54, matching RR 2.53. Not supported as worded: (1) Parekh 3.12 (1.40-6.97) and 2.63 (1.07-6.46) are for frequent cannabis use together with combustible-cigarette use or with e-cigarette use, against people who did not use cannabis (e17); the magnitude gives them as use with combustible cigarettes and with e-cigarettes, without 'frequent' or the comparison group (Page does not restate the threshold there; its earlier sentence defines frequent use as more than 10 days a month). (2) The magnitude labels Hemachandra's 3.3 'unadjusted'; Page gives it only as the estimate before adjustment for stroke-related covariates, without saying whether it was crude. (3) 'In-hospital' for Johnson-Sasso's OR 0.79 is not stated in Page (the reference title says short-term outcomes in patients hospitalised for myocardial infarction), and no interval or adjustment is printed. Missing for balance: Page reports (e17; Table 3, e11) that cannabis use, present in 6% of patients aged 50 or younger with a heart attack, is associated with worse all-cause and cardiovascular mortality (DeFilippis et al. 2018, 2,097 young adults: adjusted HR 1.99 and 2.22, given in the table for cocaine and marijuana use together); the claim's evidence after a heart attack lists only a non-significant estimate (Frost) and a lower one (Johnson-Sasso). Page also qualifies the mortality gradient relayed from Hall & Degenhardt (2.5 and 4.2 times): smaller studies (refs 37 and 87, Frost 2013 and Mukamal 2008) showed a signal toward higher mortality, but many findings were not statistically significant (e17). And Table 3 lists a 2019 systematic review (Richards et al.) in which 28 of 33 studies suggested a higher risk of acute coronary syndrome and chronic cardiovascular disease (e12).

claims.overstatement: None in the claim, which does not cite Volkow by name. Volkow's own wording is causal and one-sided: use is associated with vascular conditions that 'increase the risks' of heart attack, stroke and transient ischaemic attack during intoxication, with no estimates and no mention of null findings.
claims.note: Volkow is not named anywhere in the statement or magnitude; if this anchor stays, name Volkow et al. (2014) among the narrative reviews, or drop the anchor. The passage is second-hand (ref 45, a 2014 cardiology review by its title; the coronary-microcirculation statement cites refs 46 and 47, the latter a case report by its title). Table 2 does not rate cardiovascular effects.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of the association: 'modestly higher odds' and the association wording are more cautious than the authors' own Key Points and Conclusions. Points to fix: (1) The clause that the 7.2% attributable figure 'is not a result of its data' is not supported. The article gives no method, but the figure reproduces exactly as Levin's formula applied to the review's own pooled OR 1.37, treated as a relative risk, and the 20.9% of US adolescents reporting past-month use cited in the same paragraph: 0.209 x 0.37 / (1 + 0.209 x 0.37) = 7.18% (editors' reconstruction). Suggested wording: 'is given without a method; it matches the pooled OR treated as a relative risk combined with the share of US adolescents reporting any past-month use, although the OR compares the heaviest-use category with no use, and it assumes the link is causal.' (2) Selective qualifiers that both lean toward the null, i.e. an understatement. The claim cites the external propensity-score analysis in which the association lost significance (Harder et al.) but not the review's own propensity-score reanalysis of the Marmorstein-Iacono cohort, in which it held (OR 2.6, 1.2 to 5.5; multivariable 2.5, 1.1 to 5.5). It also says six of the 24 unpooled studies found no association without saying that the review describes most of the 24 as positive (18 cited, though one of them, ref 34, is also in the pooled set and one, ref 50, is a meta-analysis of children's peer relations). (3) Comparator: 'compared with adolescents who did not use cannabis' is the review's pooling rule (highest frequency category against non-users) for studies reporting several frequencies. For the study whose exposure is a cannabis use disorder by 17, the review does not state the comparison group.
claims.note: Every number from this source checks against the text and Figure 2: 1.37 (1.16 to 1.62), I2 0%, 7 studies; study estimates 1.44, 1.50, 1.10, 1.30, 1.48, 2.62, 1.02 (range 1.02 to 2.62), with 2 of 7 CIs excluding 1 (Brook 2002, Marmorstein 2011); 1.40 (1.17 to 1.67) without Degenhardt 2013; structured diagnosis 1.38 (1.15 to 1.66) against scales 1.28 (0.83 to 1.97); USA 1.54 (1.20 to 1.98) against other countries 1.24 (0.99 to 1.56); anxiety 1.18 (0.84 to 1.67), I2 42%, 3 studies. Countries per Figure 2: USA (2 studies), USA and Puerto Rico, Canada, UK, Australia, Australia and New Zealand, as the claim says. Recomputed DerSimonian-Laird pools from the printed rows: depression 1.37 (1.16 to 1.62); without Degenhardt 1.40 (1.18 to 1.67); structured 1.39 (1.16 to 1.67); scales 1.25 (0.79 to 1.99); USA 1.55 (1.20 to 2.00); others 1.24 (0.99 to 1.56); anxiety 1.18 (0.85 to 1.65). All match within rounding. The printed depression heterogeneity is internally inconsistent: Q = 3.26 with df 6 would give P = .78, not the printed .62; the rows give Q = 4.40 (P = .62), so the printed Q appears copied from the anxiety row (Q = 3.26, df 2, P = .20). I2 = 0% either way. 413 326 recomputed as 70 872 118 x 0.081 x 0.072 (same). The 8.1% is a 2-week prevalence in US adults aged 20 or more (ref 71), which the Discussion calls 'incidence'. 'Cannot be checked from the article' is right, and the article contradicts itself on adjustment: Statistical Analysis says all studies adjusted for prior depression and other confounders such as tobacco and alcohol; Study Selection says smoking and alcohol were controlled in 'almost all'; Limitations says not all adjusted for other drugs and cigarettes. The Narrative-review sentences (Hall & Degenhardt 2009; Hall 2015; Volkow et al. 2014) are not from this source and were not checked here.

Not supported as worded: the claim describes 'dose-response relations that lost significance after adjustment' in the Fergusson & Horwood cohort and in the Swedish conscript cohort. For the Swedish cohort, Hall (2015) reports a two-group contrast, not a dose-response: depression 1.5 times as common with the heaviest use at 18 as with no use, no longer significant after adjustment (ref 108). Suggested wording: '...in one birth cohort (frequency of use by 16), and an association that lost significance after adjustment in the Swedish conscript cohort (depression 1.5 times as common with the heaviest use at 18 as with none)'. The rest is supported: the link with depression is weaker than with psychosis (ref 107, a 2012 book chapter by the same group), OR 1.49 (1.15-1.94) with weak support for causation. Not in the claim: a combined analysis of four Australasian cohorts reached similar conclusions (ref 110), and Table 1 rates the evidence +? with probable confounding.

claims.overstatement: None.
claims.note: The statement concerns regular use in general and cites one cohort of young people (ref 23, Patton et al. 2002); Table 2 gives depression or anxiety medium confidence, by no stated method, which the claim need not repeat.

claims.overstatement: None for this source. Association wording; the claim itself gives the limits that matter (three studies per pool, two of three in each measured in adolescence, against the review's own criterion of young adulthood; the single young-adult ideation estimate 1.10, 0.58 to 2.07). Two further points could be added: only 1 of the 3 ideation estimates is individually significant (Weeks and Colman, a sample with no recent history of depression by its title), and the same Canadian study is in both pools. The Discussion's 'especially suicidal ideation' is the authors' wording, not used by the claim.
claims.note: All numbers check against the Abstract and Figure 3: ideation 1.50 (1.11 to 2.03), I2 0%, Q = 1.49, df = 2, P = .48; study estimates 1.40 (0.70 to 2.80, Fergusson 1996, New Zealand), 1.10 (0.58 to 2.07, McGee 2005, New Zealand, young adulthood), 1.74 (1.16 to 2.60, Weeks and Colman, Canada); attempts 3.46 (1.53 to 7.84), I2 61.3%, Q = 5.38, df = 2, P = .07; study estimates 4.81 (1.82 to 12.66, Roberts 2010, USA), 6.83 (2.04 to 22.90, Silins 2014, Australia and New Zealand, young adulthood), 1.87 (1.09 to 3.22, Weeks and Colman). Countries as the claim says. Most precise attempt estimate confirmed (log CI width: Weeks and Colman 1.08, Roberts 1.94, Silins 2.42). DerSimonian-Laird recomputation from the rows: ideation 1.50 (1.10 to 2.04), Q 1.47; attempts 3.48 (1.51 to 8.03), Q 5.39, I2 62.9%, within rounding. Weeks and Colman is dated 2016 in Figure 3 and 2017 in the reference list. The second-hand material (Hall & Degenhardt 2009; Hall 2015: case-control study, prospective studies, earlier meta-analysis) is not from this source and was not checked here.

claims.overstatement: None of substance; the claim is more cautious than the source, whose Results text calls the 30% responder result and the Brief Pain Inventory result greater reductions although both intervals include no difference. Minor points: 'adults' is not stated in the main text; 'mostly nabiximols' holds for the pooled analyses (7 of 8 and 6 of 6 trials) but nabiximols was 13 of the 28 trials, the largest single group, not most of them.
claims.note: Every number re-found in Results › Chronic Pain, Table 2 and Figure 2. The abstract's 37% and 31% are the crude summed proportions of Figure 2's overall row: 254/685 = 37.1% and 215/685 = 31.4%, a difference of 5.7 per 100 (editors' 'about 6 more in 100': same); 685 + 685 = 1370 patients, as in Table 2. So the derivation, though not described in words, can be reconstructed from Figure 2. Moderate-rated outcomes: 30% responders OR 1.41 (0.99 to 2.00), NRS -0.46 (-0.80 to -0.11), BPI -0.17 (-0.50 to 0.16), Neuropathic Pain Scale -3.89 (-7.32 to -0.47) on 0 to 100, EQ-5D -0.01 (-0.05 to 0.02): the claim's 'not statistically significant or small' is accurate. No minimal clinically important difference is named in the main text (the protocol is in a supplement not read). The nabiximols-only subtotal for 30% responders is OR 1.32 (0.94 to 1.86), 7 trials (Figure 2), not in the claim.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of benefit; three errors of detail. (1) Barthel index: -0.58 (-1.73 to 0.56) is not a 4-trial estimate. Table 2 prints three unlabelled estimates in that cell beside the labels Nabilone (2), Dronabinol (1), THC/CBD (1): -0.58 (-1.73 to 0.56), 0.23 (-0.13 to 0.59) and -0.03 (-0.39 to 0.33). Figure 3 shows that this layout gives one estimate per cannabinoid, not an overall (see (2)), so -0.58 is the nabilone estimate from 2 trials. A pool of all four could not have an interval of plus or minus 1.15 when two of its parts have intervals of plus or minus 0.36. The review gives no overall Barthel estimate. All three intervals include zero, so 'did not change' stands. (2) The magnitude's 'Table 2 still prints -0.11, -0.23 to 0.02' presents that figure as an uncorrected overall. Figure 3 shows -0.11 (-0.23 to 0.02) is the nabiximols subtotal (4 trials, 383 vs 337 patients), printed beside the label Nabiximols (4). The other two Table 2 values are the dronabinol (-0.94) and THC/CBD (-0.32) arms of Zajicek 2003. The corrected overall, -0.12 (-0.24 to 0.01), is in the abstract, the Results text and Figure 3. (3) 'The outcome rated moderate (Ashworth)': the review rated three spasticity outcomes moderate (Ashworth, Barthel index, walking speed), and none showed a clear difference, which strengthens the claim's point. Smaller points: 'on 0 to 10 scales' for patient-rated spasticity is not stated for that pool (Table 2 says NRS or VAS scores; the text says numerical rating scales). '1,244 people' matches Table 2, but Figure 3's overall row counts 590 + 544 = 1,134. 'Mostly nabiximols' is 6 of 14 trials. Follow-up is printed only for some spasticity outcomes (3 to 15 weeks).
claims.note: Re-found: 14 studies (2280), MS 11 (2138), paraplegia 3 (142), only MS studies pooled; risk of bias low 2, unclear 5, high 7. Patient-rated spasticity -0.76 (-1.38 to -0.14), 3 trials (698), I2 73, low; global impression OR 1.44 (1.07 to 1.94), 3 (461), low; Ashworth overall -0.12 (-0.24 to 0.01), 5 trials, I2 0, moderate, corrected online July 13 2015 per the article's correction footnote; 50% reduction OR 1.40 (0.81 to 2.41) and 30% reduction OR 1.64 (0.95 to 2.83), 2 trials (519) each, low; walking speed -0.86 (-3.08 to 1.36), 2 (497), moderate. Figure 3 also shows Zajicek 2003 entering the overall Ashworth pool twice (dronabinol and THC/CBD arms against the same 207 placebo patients; combined weight 1.7%), against the review's stated rule of one data set per study; the effect on the estimate is negligible (-0.11 to -0.12).

claims.overstatement: None; the claim labels the statement as a narrative review's and second-hand.
claims.note: The efficacy statement cites a single 1975 trial (ref 59, Sallan et al.); the statement that patients often find marijuana more effective carries no citation. The suggestion that other compounds may enhance THC's effect cites a study in the house musk shrew (ref 60, by its title). The Limitations section also relays that the 1999 Institute of Medicine report acknowledged potential benefits for chemotherapy nausea and vomiting while urging research on synthetic or pure cannabinoids.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim keeps the source's association wording, gives the review team's low GRADE rating, and says the active-comparator trials were not pooled. One small misplacement of a number: the source's '15 studies' with prochlorperazine counts every trial with a prochlorperazine arm, including 2 three-arm THC trials that also had placebo (Table 1), so prochlorperazine was the comparator in 13 of the 20 active-only trials, not 15. The claim could add that the review says, without pooling, that all trials favoured cannabinoids over both active comparators and placebo, not significantly in all.
claims.note: Numbers re-found: 28 studies, 1772 participants; nabilone 14, THC 6, levonantradol 4, dronabinol 3, nabiximols 1; risk of bias high 23, unclear 5; 8 placebo-controlled (3 of them also with an active arm), 20 active only; pooled complete response OR 3.82 (1.55 to 9.42), 3 parallel-group trials, 102 patients, dronabinol 2 and nabiximols 1, I2 0%, GRADE low. Editors' arithmetic 47 - 20 = 27 per 100: same. The 47% and 20% appear only in the abstract and the article has no forest plot for this outcome, so their derivation cannot be checked; for pain the abstract's percentages equal summed events over summed patients in Figure 2, so these are probably crude summed proportions too. As a check, an OR of 3.82 applied to a 20% placebo rate implies about 49%, consistent with 47%.

claims.overstatement: Slight understatement of what the survey reported: the claim gives only the 2 of 19 families reporting freedom from seizures, while the same survey had 8 of 19 (42%) reporting a reduction of more than 80% and 6 of 19 (32%) a reduction of 25% to 60%. All are parent reports from a small self-selected survey, which the claim could say instead of giving one outcome. 'Describes only a parent survey' is right for human data; the box also cites animal evidence for cannabidiol.
claims.note: Recomputed: 2/19 = 10.5% (printed 11%), 8/19 = 42.1% (42%), 6/19 = 31.6% (32%). The statement on insufficient safety and efficacy data concerns cannabis botanicals (ref 73), not cannabidiol medicines. The animal-model citation (ref 74) is, by its title, a study of cannabidivarin-rich extracts, not of cannabidiol.

claims.overstatement: None; the claim is more cautious than the review, whose conclusions call the evidence low quality but suggestive of improvement for HIV weight gain, sleep disorders and Tourette syndrome, and speak of 'no effect' on psychosis and depression where the claim correctly says the intervals are too wide. The framing 'too few, small or short to show whether they help' is the editors' summary; it agrees with the review's own call for larger trials in exactly these conditions and its remark that the small trials may have lacked power.
claims.note: All numbers re-found. Sleep-apnoea trial: the review and Table 2 attribute it to nabilone, but the only sleep-apnoea report in the reference list is ref 18 (Prasad et al., 2011, a conference abstract of a dronabinol trial). The 2 sleep studies' 5 reports are ref 18 plus the four reports of the fibromyalgia nabilone-amitriptyline trial (refs 63, 64, 89, 90), and Table 1 lists sleep among the indications of dronabinol against placebo; the claim's parenthesis is supported. Table 2 gives the sleep-quality pool as 8 trials (539 patients) and the sleep-disturbance pool as 3 trials (1637 patients); the two patient counts look transposed or otherwise wrong, and neither is in the claim. The depression rows in Table 2 (HADS 0.15, MADRS 1.90, BDI 0.69, single trials) and the text's highest-dose result (2.50, 0.38 to 4.62) are as the claim gives them.

claims.overstatement: 'Increase' is acceptable for randomized comparisons, and the claim names the highest-dose choice and the short-term limit. One sentence goes too far: 'The review reports odds ratios only, not how many people in 100 had each effect' holds for Table 3, but for 'any adverse event' Figure 4 prints event counts for every study and in total (1438/1779 with cannabinoids vs 1058/1710 with comparators, crude 81% vs 62%, editors' arithmetic). Suggested: 'apart from the counts for any adverse event in a forest plot, the review reports odds ratios only'. Also note that the comparators in the AE pools include active drugs: Figure 4's 'placebo' column includes active-comparator trials, as Table 3's title says.
claims.note: All odds ratios, intervals, study and patient counts re-found in Table 3; I2 31% (any), 0% (serious), 2% (withdrawal). AE data in 62 studies (127 reports). risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence checklist, editors' summary low, holds for the cannabis figures as for stimulants: national probability sample, 82.4% response, standardized CIDI applied identically across drug classes, design-based standard errors. interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the abstract gives only aggregates; 'transition' language invites a risk reading the cross-sectional ratio does not support; the 20-40% statement does not fit cocaine.

missed: The card was written for methamphetamine and has no finding for the cannabis values the two cannabis claims now rest on: Table 2 (p. 251) cannabis lifetime use 46.3% (SE 1.1) and dependence 4.2% (0.3), with 9.1% (0.7) among users; Table 4 (p. 256) dependence among users by age at interview 15.3% (2.3), 8.1% (0.7), 8.5% (1.3) and 3.1% (1.5); Table 5 (p. 259) men 12.0% (1.1) and women 5.5% (0.7); the text restates these on p. 254 (46.3% and 9.1%; 1 dependent for every 10 not, p. 255) and p. 264 (12% and 5.5%). All five gaps verified (Key Points and Discussion 1st paragraph present 47% as the share who will experience withdrawal; Conclusions on men; Abstract › Importance calls withdrawal a diagnostic indicator of use disorder; Discussion 2nd paragraph on symptoms mistaken for anxiety or depression).

missed: Figure 2 (forest plot, an image) gives estimates the card does not record: random effects overall 0.46 (0.37 to 0.55); fixed effect overall 0.28 (0.27 to 0.28) and by setting 0.19, 0.52 and 0.82; event counts summing to 6,469 (3,245; 2,929; 295). interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The Primer is mostly hedged; the main stretches are those the card lists. I would add the relabelling of Bahji's withdrawal figures (see missed).

missed: Management > Cannabis withdrawal, 1st paragraph: the Primer gives Bahji et al.'s pooled figures (ref. 203) as the prevalence 'in the general population of cannabis users' (12-17%) and as the share of treatment-seeking patients with CUD reporting 'clinically severe' withdrawal (54% of outpatients, 87% of inpatients). missed: Box 1 (p. 294) says all IQ studies 'ignored possible residual effects of the drug on IQ test performance'. For Dunedin this is not so: Broyd et al. (2016, AM p. 9) describe Meier et al. (2012) as ruling out recent cannabis use, and the teen-IQ claim reports the sensitivity analysis leaving out use in the day or week before testing. risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high follows from the confounding domain: adjustment for measured confounders roughly halves every odds ratio, and family history, genetic liability, childhood adversity, premorbid functioning and use during a prodrome were not addressed. Exposure measurement at some concerns is defensible, though retrospective recall after onset, with potency inferred from the name of the type, could justify high; it does not change the overall judgment.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' fits, and points (1) to (7) are accurate against the text (Discussion, 3rd paragraph calls high-potency use a strong predictor in Paris; Discussion, 11th paragraph says unmentioned recruitment materials avoid selection and recall bias). One addition: the Results also use causal and risk wording for odds ratios (high-potency use increased the odds, 8th paragraph; a doubling of risk, 8th paragraph; a fourfold increase in risk, 9th paragraph).

missed: Every site-level attributable-fraction interval in Table 3 lies above zero, including 15 site estimates whose odds-ratio interval includes 1, so reporting issue 10 applies to the whole table, not only to the three entries marked significant.

'Mainly' high- or low-potency use (key finding 6, can_establish, analysis, interpretation_gap) is not in the main text, which speaks of lifetime use of cannabis by potency; the rule for classing people who used both types is only in the appendix. Drop 'mainly' or cite the appendix after reading it.

The Discussion (1st paragraph) says early first use did not raise the odds independently of frequency or potency, but no estimate for first use at 15 or younger adjusted for daily use or potency is printed; only the reverse adjustment (daily use 3.1, 2.1-5.2, after adding age at first use) and the high-potency-by-15 estimate (2.3, 1.4-3.1) are given.

Current use at assessment was not associated after full adjustment (1.1, 0.9-1.5, p = 0.36; in key finding 3), which matters for claims that speak of people who use cannabis without saying that the exposure is a lifetime pattern; worth stating in the exposure field beside the definition of lifetime frequency.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high, following the worst domain (no systematic search or selection). The domain notes match the text; authorship overlap checked against the printed reference list (Zammit on refs 10, 12, 21, 37, 38, 46, 65, 67; Gage on 23, 49, 57, 65; Hickman on 23, 49, 57, 65, 67).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The contrast the card notes between 'specificity ... in some studies but not all' (AM p. 10) and 'all met' (AM p. 11) is accurate.

missed.item: Minor: the ECA estimate in Table 1, 2.0 (1.25-3.12), differs in its interval from the same daily-use estimate in Moore et al. (2007), Figure 2, 2.00 (1.27-3.16).
missed.consequence: Small transcription difference; cite the ECA figure from Moore et al. or the primary paper, not from Gage's Table 1.

risk_of_bias.note: High overall for the forward estimate is defensible: the exclusion restriction is untested (the authors themselves name impulsivity and risk taking), MR-Egger is null and imprecise, and the positive control failed. The claim cites the reverse estimate too, for which the card's own judgment is some concerns; the claim's reasoning should carry that split. Editors' F >= about 20 per variant from p < 10^-5 recomputed (chi-square 19.51).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The authors' wording is hedged ('some evidence', 'small'); the main stretch is calling the reverse result strong evidence for the reverse-causation hypothesis, which the card lists as gap (3).

missed: Discussion > Strengths and limitations, 5th paragraph: the reverse analysis assumes that schizophrenia variants act on behaviour in the general population, most of whom never develop schizophrenia (authors cite the psychosis continuum and childhood psychopathology findings). This bears directly on the claim's reading that genetic liability to schizophrenia makes cannabis use more likely.

Discussion > Strengths and limitations, 7th paragraph: MR-Egger tests biological (horizontal) pleiotropy only, not mediated pleiotropy, and the authors note that a genetic correlation (Verweij et al.) fits shared genetic architecture or causation in either direction; relevant to the claim's 'shared genetic liability' alternative.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high (no search or selection). The 'reliance on own studies' concern is apt: the only co-relative study, which carries the 'more than half' statement, has Kendler as last author, and the viewpoint reports no conflicts.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor, as the conclusion is hedged. The card's point (2) is the strongest: by footnote a's own criterion, telling hypothesis 2 from 3 needs a monozygotic OR significantly above 1, which was not tested (footnote e), yet the Table marks the discordant-pair column 'Hypotheses 2' only; 'good evidence against hypothesis 3' is the most stretched statement in the conclusions.

missed.item: Minor: the card's interpretation-gap summary calls the co-relative study a 'registry study'; the viewpoint does not say so (nor that it was Swedish). The Swedish national design is in the study's full title as cited by Gage et al. (2016), ref. 26.
missed.consequence: If 'Swedish registry' is kept in cl_can_psychosis_causation, it should be anchored to the primary paper (Giordano et al., 2015) or to Gage et al.'s reference, not to this viewpoint.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall critically low agreed: items 2, 4 (under senior decision 21) and 15 fail on their own. Single-domain differences: item 13 'no' is a close call that this reader would judge 'yes' by the item's wording, because the Limitations and the 2nd paragraph of Results › Sensitivity Analysis discuss the likely effect of confounding (incomplete adjustment for drugs, tobacco and psychosocial factors; residual confounding by depression), even though the Key Points and Conclusions ignore it. Item 9 'partial-yes' is defensible; the RTI item bank covers confounding, selection, measurement and reporting, so the technique alone would meet 'yes', and the missing ratings bear on items 12 and 13. One wording point in the reasoning: 'the attributable-case figure is not a result of the review's data' conflicts with the card's own key finding 12 and interpretation_gap point 2, which show the figure applies the pooled OR, as a relative risk, to an outside prevalence. interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' is right. Points 1 to 7 are all borne out by the text and Figures 1 to 3 as read by this reader.

missed: Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph states that all studies reported ORs adjusted for prior depression and other confounders, e.g., sex, tobacco smoking and alcohol. This is the strongest of three inconsistent statements on adjustment (Study Selection: 'almost all'; Limitations: 'not all'); add it to reporting issue 9 and key finding 2.

Comparator for the cannabis use disorder study: the review pools the highest frequency category against non-users only for studies that reported several categories. For Marmorstein and Iacono (exposure a cannabis use disorder by 17), the article does not say who the comparison group was, so 'against no use' (design_detail, comparison.controls, key finding 4 note) is not established for that study.

Wording carried into claim cl_can_teen_depression_anxiety: the risk_of_bias reasoning's 'not a result of the review's data' became the claim's 'is not a result of its data'. Both should follow key finding 12: no stated method; it applies the pooled OR, treated as a relative risk, to the share of US adolescents with any past-month use; it assumes causation.
Minor: Weeks and Colman are dated 2016 in Figure 3 but 2017 in the reference list (ref 57); the card follows the figure.

key_findings_flagged.correction: The source names tobacco and HEAVY alcohol use as established causes of low birth weight, preterm birth and small for gestational age (Discussion, 6th paragraph); the finding's 'tobacco and alcohol, which are established causes' drops 'heavy'. The same word is missing from the claim cl_can_pregnancy_birth.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low is secure: items 11 (raw means and SDs pooled, no statement that any OR was adjusted) and 15 (publication bias not assessed) are critical flaws on the main text alone, and item 7 (860 full-text exclusions without list or reasons) is a third. Items 2 and 9 as partial yes are defensible; the protocol-dependent parts of item 2 were not checked by this reader.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract's 'may increase adverse outcomes' and Discussion 3rd paragraph's causal wording on low birth weight sit against the authors' own statement that a cannabis-only effect could not be separated from tobacco and alcohol; the abstract leads with anaemia, which the Discussion says rests on one study; the 'high quality' verdict is unsupported in the main text.

missed: Figure 1 also gives the number of distinct studies across the odds-ratio pools (12) and across the mean-difference pools (10); not on the card (minor).
Methods › Assessment of heterogeneity: I2 was calculated only for Q-test p at or below 0.10, which bears on reporting issue 5 (see note there).

For the claim editor: the claim cl_can_pregnancy_birth calls the pooled estimates 'crude', which is firmer than the card's own, accurate wording (the paper does not say whether any pooled OR was adjusted; the mean differences are unadjusted by construction). 'No adjustment stated' is exact; 'crude' is certain only for the four mean-difference pools.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: Correction: the dose qualifier does appear in the body, as an uncited statement in the potency paragraph (p. 1389: high THC content can increase psychotic symptoms in people new to cannabis), though not in the acute-effects text, which links psychotic symptoms to inexperience. The 10-year threshold has no basis in the body beyond the Yücel et al. sample. The consequence stands: neither qualifier rests on evidence presented in the review.

risk_of_bias.note: Domain facts checked: 5 of 96 references have an author of the review (refs 2, 5, 68, 77, 88); refs 18 and 48 are chapters in a book Hall co-edited; a rough count of superscripts in the text extraction gives about 18 citations of ref 5 and 9 of ref 9, as the card says. missed: No figure of 25-50% for dependence among people who use daily appears anywhere in the review (text, panels, conclusions), although Volkow et al. (2014) cite this review for one (used in cl_can_dependence_frequency_onset). The card should say so under KF 3 or KF 8 so that the figure is not traced back here. The same figure appears, with no citation on the sentence, in Page et al. (2020, p. e13).

Withdrawal (KF 9): the review lists anxiety, insomnia, appetite disturbance and depression among the symptoms people seeking help report, without ranking them; the ranking 'most common' is Hall (2015, p. 5). Relevant because cl_can_withdrawal attributes 'most often' to this review.

key_findings_flagged.correction: The review says the 1980s-1990s meta-analysis suggested (not found) that regular use in pregnancy reduced birth weight (p. 3). Add from p. 4: under-reporting of use probably attenuates the associations with poor birth outcomes, and cigarette smoking has often been hard to adjust for fully.

The finding is right; the note is not. School leaving is not the review's only discordant-twin test of a causal claim: the Other drug use section (p. 7) reports discordant-twin studies (Lynskey et al. 2003; US and Dutch studies, both cited to ref 86) in which the association with other illicit drug use persisted within pairs. risk_of_bias.note: Checked: 16 references name Hall, 13 as an author (refs 2, 6, 9, 11, 41, 49, 51, 70, 84, 98, 107, 157, 163) and 3 chapters in a book he co-edited (refs 14, 134, 139), as the card says; Rogeberg (2013) is not cited; literature searches are mentioned only in the acknowledgements. missed: Pregnancy (KF 5): the review's statement that under-reporting probably attenuates the associations, and that cigarette smoking is often hard to adjust for fully (p. 4). The claim cl_can_pregnancy_birth uses both points, the first without its direction.

The family-history qualifier in the psychosis conclusion (p. 12) repeats a 1993 conclusion listed among the acute effects on pp. 2-3 (psychotic symptoms at high doses, especially with a personal or family history of psychosis); no new evidence for it is presented, which supports the card's note on KF 27.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Replace '6 men' with '6 participants (N = 6; the review does not state their sex)'. Everything else confirmed at 2.1.1, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs, and the Fig. 1 and 2 legends.

(1982) (references 21 and 95); only the split of more than 65% in feces and about 20% in urine is cited to Wall et al. (1983). interpretation_gap.note: Minor. All four points verified at the stated places (3.1.5, 3rd paragraph; 3.1.5, 1st paragraph; 2.2, 4th and 6th paragraphs; 3.2, 1st, and 3.2.2, 5th paragraphs).

missed: The '6 men' error also appears in sample.recruitment ('6 men smoking cigarettes of 1.75% and 3.55% THC') and underlies 'small groups of men' in cannot_establish; the review gives sex only for some studies (eight males IV, 20 male volunteers, 38 males in the hair study; women and men in Wall et al.).

3.2, 1st paragraph: a naive user's urine may test negative by immunoassay within a few hours after one cigarette; a useful lower bound beside the 67- and 93-day cases.

Funding field confirmed: the author-information panel gives the affiliation as Chemistry and Drug Metabolism, Intramural Research Program, NIDA, NIH, Baltimore, and the manuscript has no funding, acknowledgement or conflict statement.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: Partly checked: the year-of-age analysis's n of 785 and 2,271, against 789 and 2,277, is confirmed. interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract and conclusion read imprecise, non-significant co-twin differences as showing that the association is not causal; 'completely eliminated' overstates −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6); and the baseline-difference argument holds in only one cohort.

missed: Balance for key finding 8 and the interpretation gap: in the largest discordant group, MTFS DZ pairs (99), the Vocabulary interval (0.2, −2.8 to 3.3) excludes the between-family difference of −3.4. risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high (search, separation of evidence from speculation, balance). No reference has Ksir or Hart as author, so 'low' for reliance on own studies is right.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. The card's point (6) holds: monozygotic co-twins share season of birth, so it cannot explain a residual within-pair association. Also, the review presents an uncontrolled national time trend as a 'semi-experimental' test (p. 8).

key_findings_flagged.correction: Numbers right, meaning to be stated: the source says half of the cases of dependence were observed about 27 (nicotine), 13 (alcohol), 5 (cannabis) and 4 (cocaine) years after first use, i.e. medians among people who became dependent, read from Figure 1, not the time by which half of users became dependent. reporting_issues_flagged.note: Issue confirmed (every Table 1 stratification sums to 16,053, 29,160, 7,409 and 2,263). risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence, editors' summary moderate, fits the cumulative transition probabilities that cl_can_dependence_how_many uses. The cannabis onset claim now uses the paper's hazard ratios, an exposure association; for that use a ROBINS-E appraisal would be needed (confounding; time-varying psychiatric and substance use disorders as possible mediators; survivors only; recalled onset ages), which this card does not provide.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor overall. One gap matters for the cannabis claims: the Discussion reads the reversal of early onset as the higher risk being 'mostly explained by' psychiatric and substance use covariates, treating time-varying disorders that may follow early use as confounders; and it cites socio-economic adjustment, though the cannabis model retained no socioeconomic term. Also, results_show says family history predicted transition across substances; in the adjusted models it was retained only for nicotine and alcohol.

missed: The cannabis column of Table 4 in full: male 1.44 (1.1-1.9); age 18-29 3.09 (1.9-4.9) and 30-44 2.46 (1.7-3.5) against 45+; American Indian or Alaska Native 1.91 (1.2-3.0); mood 2.69 (1.9-3.9); anxiety 2.31 (1.6-3.4); personality 2.3 (1.7-3.1); nicotine dependence 2.06 (1.4-3.1); alcohol 2.55 (1.8-3.5); cocaine 4.14 (2.3-7.6); onset before 14 0.63 (0.5-0.9). The Discussion's own alternative for the onset reversal (7th paragraph): people who start later may have more intense use and greater availability, affordability and acceptance in late adolescence.
The paper calls its 5.9% at a decade consistent with the NCS estimate, which its Introduction gives as 8% for cannabis within a decade (Wagner & Anthony, 2002).
Figure 1 in this manuscript has no key to its symbols; the curves can be identified only by matching their plateaus with the text.
Methods 2.1 lists the deceased, deported, impaired and military as 'eligible' where ineligible is evidently meant; the Wave 1 dates (2001-2002) appear only in a reference title, not in the text.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low: protocol, excluded-study list, risk-of-bias assessment and its use in interpretation, and appropriate (adjusted) pooling are all missing; items 4 and 5 are close calls as the card says, and either reading leaves several critical flaws.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' fits; the quoted phrases (abstract; Discussion, 9th paragraph) and points (1) to (6) are accurate against the text and figures. One addition: the Methods state that never users were always the reference category, but Table 1 shows other reference groups in some studies (see missed).

missed: Reference groups: Methods > Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph says never users were consistently the reference, but Table 1's reference rows are 'No cannabis within last year' (Wiles 2006), 'None' or 'No use' for frequency at baseline (Henquet 2005, Degenhardt 2001) and 'No cannabis use at age 18' (Arseneault 2002). The card's comparison field repeats the Methods statement; it should note the table, and claims should say 'against no use' rather than 'against never use'.

Crude absolute risks by level can be read from Table 1 for the six cohorts (editors' calculation; follow-up length not given in this paper): Swedish conscripts, admission for schizophrenia, 215 of 36,429 (0.59%) with no use vs 28 of 731 (3.8%) with more than 50 occasions; Dunedin, schizophreniform disorder by 26, 12 of 494 (2.4%) vs 3 of 29 (10.3%). The card's cannot_establish lists absolute risks, and the frequency claim says no source gives them; both should be qualified, with the caveat that these are crude.

In the Dunedin study the ordered levels are defined by age at first use (use by 18 vs use by 15, Table 1), so in one of the ten studies the 'level of use' is age of onset rather than amount; the exposure field's statement that age at first use was not considered needs that exception.

Overlap with Moore et al. (2007): five of the six pooled cohorts were published by 2006 (Tien 1990, Arseneault 2002, Zammit 2002, Henquet 2005, Wiles 2006), so Marconi and Moore probably share most of their cohort data (to be checked against sc_moore_2007). The two reviews should not count as independent replication in the frequency claim's status.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Not an error found in the card; part of this finding could not be checked. The text part is confirmed: excluding each group in turn left the IQ-change estimates virtually the same and significant, and the multivariable model with past-24-hour use, number of waves of tobacco, hard-drug and alcohol dependence, and schizophrenia gave t = −2.20, P = 0.0282 (Results › Is Impairment Attributable…, 1st paragraph). The excluded-group sizes (38, 89, 126, 7, 53, 28) and the full-cohort n = 874 are printed only in the Fig. 1 key, which I did not inspect before the browser became unreachable; they need a targeted check, as do the same n values repeated in the card's sample, exposure and polysubstance fields.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E, high overall, driven by confounding: the main models adjust for sex only, and no SES, family or personality covariate enters this paper. The other domain judgments fit what I read. The Fig. 1 n values cited in the missing-data and exposure notes were not checked by me (see key finding 5).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: 'cessation for a year or more', 'global' decline, 'ruled out premorbid deficit' and the 8-point figure go beyond the tabulated results, as the card sets out.

missed: The test behind the p values printed on Figs. 2 and 3 (the onset contrasts within each persistence level and the child-against-adult comparisons) is not described in the Methods, so it is not known how they were computed or whether they are sex-adjusted like the trend tests. Key finding 8 could also say in so many words that p = .02 is a printed between-onset test at 3 or more waves, since one claim states that no such test was made.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: The wording is not merely ambiguous; it is wrong on two points. (1) The Discussion says the decline was 'from age 18–38', but Meier et al. (2012) measured IQ change from childhood (mean of ages 7-13) to 38 and had no IQ test at 18 (Meier 2012, Methods › Statistical Analysis). (2) It says that people dependent only at 18 'did not show IQ decline'. In Meier 2012 Fig. 2, the matching group (dependence before 18 at one wave, n = 17) changed by about −0.22 SD (about 3 points), not significantly different from adult onset (p = .44); no test against no change is reported. The 8 points refers to the 23 adolescent-onset people with dependence at 3 or more waves, read from a figure. Suggested issue text: the Discussion misstates the time frame and the single-wave result of the 2012 Dunedin paper; take Dunedin figures from Meier et al. (2012) itself.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E some concerns overall, judged for the within-pair estimates, with no domain high. The main limit on the null results is imprecision rather than bias, which the card states, and GRADE should take it up under imprecision. The full-sample comparisons that the claims also cite (lower IQ at 5 and 12; change −1.73) are adjusted only for sex; that is acceptable for describing pre-existing differences.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Minor' is acceptable given the stated limits. The abstract's 'Family background factors explain why adolescent cannabis users perform worse' states as established what rests on 57 pooled MZ/DZ discordant pairs, with no intervals and with non-shared confounders unmeasured; 'are consistent with family background explaining' would match the data.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Not checked rather than wrong. The text part is confirmed: middle-class families only, excluding low- and high-SES families, beta −0.155, t −3.61, P = 0.0003 (3rd paragraph). The n of 553 and the bar values (about −0.37 against −0.38) appear only on Fig. 2, which I could not view; targeted check needed. Not checked rather than wrong. The whole finding (group sizes 9/32, 8/10, 17/8 and bar heights) rests on Fig. 3B, which I could not view. The caption confirms only that panel B shows the same pattern as panel A, with no p values. Targeted check needed. If the sizes are right, the middle-class age-of-onset cells total 84.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: Not checked rather than wrong. The text part is confirmed: low-SES IQ said not to change 'from the beginning of schooling to adolescence'. The figure detail on which the issue rests (Fig. 1 starts at age 7, with no group sizes or error bars) could not be viewed. Meier et al. (2012) say childhood IQ was tested at 7, 9, 11 and 13, which fits. Targeted check needed.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E high, driven by confounding. On the narrow question (do SES as classified or childhood self-control explain the association?), the tests are direct and use measures taken before cannabis use. On the causal question, each covariate is added alone to the sex-only model.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Minor' is defensible because the tests are direct and the letter says observational studies cannot prove causation. Even so, the title ('No evidence that ... confound') and the text ('actual data exclude the possibility', 'these tests exclude') claim more than single-covariate adjustment and a three-class occupational SES measure can show; 'moderate' would also be defensible.

missed: The claim built on this reply says SES 'did not predict adolescent-onset dependence'. The source says 'did not significantly predict' (chi-square 1.15, P = 0.56), in a small group: Meier 2012's Fig. 2 has 52 people with dependence before 18. The card could note that the test had little power. That would keep 'no significant association' from being read as 'no association'.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 low confidence (provisional): one critical flaw (item 2, no protocol), item 7 not judgeable from the article. The domain judgments match what the article reports; item 11 'yes' is a close call, as the card says, because three of six most-frequent-use estimates lack adjustment for other drugs and the depression pool includes an unadjusted estimate.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible: the summary's 'independently of confounding' covers measured confounders only, and 'similar' understates the disorder estimate (2.58 vs 1.41), but the paper states its uncertainty plainly (pp. 325, 327) and labels the attributable fraction as conditional on causality.

missed.item: Table 1 does not say which exposure contrast each 'crude to adjusted' percentage refers to, and the NPMS value cannot refer to the ever-use estimate pooled in Figure 1: with an adjusted OR of 0.72 the footnote's formula (crude - adjusted)/(crude - 1) gives more than 100% for any crude OR above 1. It fits the dependence estimate in Figure 2 (1.47) with a crude OR of about 3.35. The implied crude ORs for the other six cohorts are plausible with either contrast, so the seven percentages may mix ever-use and most-frequent-use contrasts.
missed.consequence: The 'about 45% (10%-80%)' attenuation is an average over unstated, possibly mixed contrasts; claims may cite it as a description of how much adjustment shrank the cohorts' associations, but should not attach it to the pooled ever-use OR of 1.41 in particular. Suggested as a reporting issue.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high: no search or selection criteria, no appraisal, heavy reliance on the authors' own studies (13 of 166 references by my count too), and an unbalanced treatment of shared-liability and reverse-causation evidence.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' fits and the quoted abstract phrase is exact. One wording correction: the card's '(8-24%, from the authors' own study, assuming causality)' may read as though Murray states the causal assumption; Murray states none, and presents the range as the share preventable if nobody used cannabis.

missed: The 24% in the 8-24% range is, per Di Forti et al. (2019, Research in context panel), the 2015 study's attributable fraction for high-potency cannabis, while Murray presents the range as the share of psychosis preventable if nobody used cannabis (Conclusions, 3rd paragraph), with no causal assumption stated. Murray mislabels the exposure, beyond the selection of the range that reporting issue 6 notes.

Andreasson et al. (1987): Murray's 'six times' (Psychosis, 2nd paragraph) is given without its adjustment status; from general knowledge, not from this source, it is the unadjusted relative risk for more than 50 occasions, about 2.3 after adjustment in the original paper. To be checked at the primary before any claim uses it.

Murray presents the polygenic finding on potency from its own correspondence reply (ref 90) without figures and as 'no evidence to support' the predisposition hypothesis; the card's replication timeline turns this into 'finding no difference in polygenic scores', which is stronger than the review's wording.

key_findings_flagged.correction: The statement says that many of the findings of the smaller mortality studies failed to reach statistical significance (p. e17), not that they mostly did; replace 'mostly not significant' with 'many not significant'. The rest is confirmed.

The statement does not name Colorado: it describes Crume et al. as a study in a state with legalised medical and recreational cannabis (p. e14), and the title of ref 70 names no state. Drop 'in Colorado' or source it from the primary paper. The rest is confirmed (5.7% plus or minus 0.5; 5.0%, 4.1-6.2; OR 1.5, 1.1-2.1, P=0.02; the adjustment set; Gunn et al.'s figures with the mean difference printed without a sign).

risk_of_bias.note: Checked: no funding statement is printed; Rana is a co-author of refs 29, 30 and 46; Kloner of ref 22. Overall high follows the worst domains (search, appraisal, grading).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible because the body's own conclusions (inconclusive; insufficient for people with cardiac risk factors) match the evidence. It is the upper edge of minor: the abstract's framing and the sentence attributing worse mortality to cannabis from a combined cocaine-and-marijuana estimate go beyond the statement's own table.

missed: Hyperemesis (p. e13, Chronic Side Effects, uncited sentence): long-term heavy, THC-predominant use is associated with a higher risk of hyperemesis syndrome, with prodromal abdominal discomfort and nausea leading to intractable vomiting. The card has only the Table 2 row (KF 28).

Withdrawal advice (p. e18, Patient Education and Considerations): clinicians are told to advise people who use long term and heavily not to stop suddenly, because of the risk of withdrawal syndrome, and to seek care if withdrawal or hyperemesis symptoms arise. No evidence is cited. It sits uneasily with the statement in cl_can_withdrawal (from Connor et al., 2021) that withdrawal carries no serious risk; if used, report it as the AHA's recommendation, not as evidence.

Withdrawal time course (p. e13; KF 25 has it): onset a few days after stopping, peak at about 10 days, end after about 30 days (refs 5, 12). This differs from the time course in cl_can_withdrawal (peak within the first week, fading within 1-2 weeks), which does not cite this statement; the editor may want to note the disagreement.

risk_of_bias.note: Some concerns overall, judged for the genetic correlation and the reverse MR, is defensible. The causation claim also cites the forward estimates, for which the card itself says the editors would judge high (weak instruments, risk-taking-linked lead locus CADM2, no multivariable MR). The claim's certainty reasoning should use that split.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor once the 2019 correction is applied (liability, not diagnosis). The Table 3 footnote's reading of the odds ratios as group comparisons remains, as the card lists.

missed: Figure 1 legend (b) says the GWAS test was linear regression, while Online Methods > Statistics > Genome-wide association analyses and meta-analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, say logistic regression and a meta-analysis of log odds ratios. This matters for the MR scale: the per-unit-of-log-odds reading of B assumes log-odds SNP effects.

Online Methods > Causal association between cannabis use and schizophrenia: Two-sample Mendelian randomization, 6th paragraph: the effective sample sizes used for variance explained (130,072 schizophrenia; 180,934 cannabis) cannot be reproduced from the paper's counts with its own formula 4/(1/cases + 1/controls). Editors' calculation: about 151,500 for cannabis from the three samples' reported prevalences of use, and about 111,500 for PGC2 with 36,989 cases and 113,075 controls; which schizophrenia release was used is not stated beyond ref. 66. The variance-explained figures (1.12%, 0.15%, 3.38%) are therefore approximate and may be somewhat underestimated, though the cannabis instrument stays at about 1%.

risk_of_bias.note: The editors' checklist with adapted domains, overall high, fits: the assumptions are not calibrated to Dunedin, the model was built from the confounding reading of the Meier estimates, and only the main table was compared. The 'Calibration' domain cites a Fig. 1 value I could not check, but the judgment stands without it.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Minor' is acceptable because the article hedges (results not discredited; caveats stated). But the abstract's 'likely to be overestimates' and the conclusion's 'likely biased' are probability judgments that a sufficiency simulation cannot carry. A claim should cite only 'could produce'.

missed: Rogeberg reports how often the trend test reached the 10%, 5% and 1% levels (about 60%, 50% and 30% of runs), but Meier's own trend was far stronger (t = −4.45, P < 0.0001), and the article never says how often the no-effect model produced a t that large. The simulation shows that conventional significance is common under confounding, not that a result as strong as Meier's is. Cards and claims saying the simulation 'reproduces' the Dunedin result should say so.

key_findings_flagged.correction: The finding's numbers are all correct, but its note is wrong: the more-than-72-hours interval (-0.22 to 0.07) does NOT include the overall estimate (-0.247); it overlaps the overall interval (-0.32 to -0.17) only between -0.22 and -0.17. Suggested note: 'A between-study comparison, not a within-person change. The more-than-72-hours interval includes no difference and reaches -0.22, close to the overall -0.25, so it does not exclude a deficit of nearly the overall size. The -0.30 estimate for the other 54 studies is printed only in the Abstract. The authors describe the abstinence associations as holding at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons (Discussion › Length of Abstinence and Reduction of Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph).' The same error is in interpretation_gap (point 2) and analysis.power, and was carried into claim cl_can_cognition_after_stopping.

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low under AMSTAR 2. Items 2, 7 and 9 fail on their own, so the overall rating holds even if item 4 (decided under senior decision 21) or item 11 (a close call, as the card says) were judged otherwise. Item 13 'yes' is generous, since no study was appraised and the Abstract and Key Points state the abstinence conclusion without caveats, but the Discussion does discuss confounding, pre-existing deficits and small-study bias, which meets the item's wording for non-randomized studies. Provisional, because the supplement was not read.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' is right: the Abstract, Key Points and Conclusions speak of deficits being diminished or restored with abstinence, but the evidence is a between-study, uncorrected moderator result. One correction to point (2): the more-than-72-hours interval (-0.22 to 0.07) does not include the overall estimate (-0.247). The conclusion that the result does not show that no deficit remains still holds, because the interval reaches -0.22, close to the overall value.

missed: analysis.power repeats the interval error ('whose interval (-0.22 to 0.07) includes the overall estimate'): it does not, since -0.247 lies below -0.22. Correct it together with key finding 7 and interpretation_gap point 2; claim cl_can_cognition_after_stopping carries the same wrong clause.

The authors themselves say the abstinence associations hold only at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons (Discussion › Length of Abstinence and Reduction of Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph). The card says the P = .01 test is one of several moderator analyses, but no key finding records the authors' own statement. Claims that cite P = .01 should mark it as uncorrected.

Discussion, 1st paragraph (before the first subheading): the authors cite the National Academies report (ref. 91) as concluding there is significant uncertainty about cannabis-associated cognitive deficits after sustained abstinence. It appears only in the replication timeline; as a key finding it would support the 'insufficient evidence, disputed' framing of cl_can_cognition_after_stopping (minor).

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low agreed: critical items 2, 4, 7, 9 and 13 not met (no protocol; English only from 2000; no list of excluded full texts and no flow diagram; no appraisal of included studies). Item 16 'yes' is lenient, since no statement covers funding for the review itself, but it is not critical and does not change the overall rating.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. All six gaps verified at the stated places (Cumulative Synthesis 4th paragraph; Discussion 4th, 5th and 9th paragraphs; Introduction 1st paragraph; Abstract).

missed: The two patients without resolution are attributed in the text to two case reports (references 8 and 56, Cox et al. 2012 and Parikh & Gould 2010, the latter a meeting abstract), while Table 1 places one in the Soriano-Co series (4 of 5) and one among the case reports (37 of 38); together with the Simonetto discrepancy in RI 4, the 62 of 64 is not reproducible from the source's own tables.
Table 1 heads the resolution column 'relief with abstinence or reduction', while the text calls the 64 'documented cannabis cessation'.

The median ages (n = 111, 84, 101) come only from the 113 cases with raw data: each n equals the sum of the Table 1 rows without the 98-patient Simonetto series, which reported only means (32.3 years at diagnosis, 25.3 at symptom onset).
Time to improvement of symptoms with abstinence is listed among the data extracted (Data Collection, 2nd paragraph) but no result is reported.
Return of symptoms on resuming use is counted as too inconsistently documented (Table 2), yet Table 5 relays that all 3 of Allen et al.'s patients who resumed after abstinence relapsed.
The printed percentages are truncated, not rounded: 92.3 (92.4), 96.8 (96.9), 97.4 (97.5), 74.8 (74.9), 40.2 (40.3), besides the 72.9 (73.0) noted in RI 2.
Minor: the Methods define the longest duration category as greater than 11 years, the Results and Table 1 as 11 years or more.

key_findings_flagged.note: All values come from the Figure 2 image, which I did not see (the browser became unreachable after my reading, and the text and legend give no per-variant values). Needs a targeted check. The editors' pooled 1.08 (1.02-1.14) matches the text.

risk_of_bias.note: High overall: ten sub-threshold variants explaining 1%; exclusion restriction examined for ever smoking only; reverse direction untested; Egger estimates only in the supplement, with a diluted Egger (I2 67%). Editors' F of about 33 recomputed (32.6); per-variant chi-squares 21.8 to 25.4 recomputed.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: 'strongly supports' a causal relation and 'closest approximation to a randomized trial' from a 1%-variance, sub-threshold instrument, with the reverse direction untested and a headline that depends on a rescaling given only in the supplement.

missed: Abstract: P = 0.007 is printed next to the rescaled users-vs-non-users OR 1.37; it is the p-value of the per-unit estimate (1.08), and the abstract describes the rescaled figure as if two groups had been compared directly.

By my arithmetic the rescaling from 1.08 per unit to 1.37 corresponds to a contrast of about 4.1 units in the log odds of ever use (ln 1.37 / ln 1.08), for example roughly from a 5% to a 75% probability (4.04 units) of ever use, which shows how far the headline extrapolates from the per-unit estimate (editors' calculation; the supplement's inputs were not read).

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high. No reference among the 77 lists Volkow, Baler, Compton or Weiss (my check), so 'low' for reliance on own studies is right.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. Verified: Table 1 and 2 framing as effects; 'results in measurable and long-lasting cognitive impairments' on ref 16; Solowij et al. (ref 31) a treatment-seeking sample by title; long-term exposure and driving cited to ref 35 only; high confidence in diminished achievement beside ref 33's shared environmental factors; hedged conclusions.

missed: Further citation mismatches, by reference title (extending RI 3): the box cites ref 60, a study in the house musk shrew, for other plant compounds enhancing THC's antiemetic effect; ref 74, a study of cannabidivarin-rich extracts, for cannabidiol's antiepileptic role in animals; refs 55 and 56 (endocannabinoids in human eye tissue; WIN55212-2) for THC, cannabinol and nabilone, but not cannabidiol, lowering intraocular pressure in rabbits; and ref 58, a review of cannabidiol, for THC's early use against chemotherapy nausea.
Box › Nausea: the statement that patients often find marijuana more effective than THC carries no citation.
RISK OF ADDICTION: that withdrawal makes stopping difficult and contributes to relapse rests on ref 5, a paper on diagnostic criteria by its title.

Funding field confirmed: the author-information panel gives all four authors at the National Institute on Drug Abuse, NIH, Bethesda; the footnotes state no potential conflict of interest; no funding statement.

key_findings_flagged.correction: '20 against an active drug only, most often prochlorperazine (15 studies)': the source's 15 counts every trial with a prochlorperazine arm among the 23 with an active comparator; Table 1 shows 2 of them (THC against placebo and prochlorperazine) also had a placebo arm, so prochlorperazine was the comparator in 13 of the 20 active-only trials. Suggested: 'prochlorperazine was the comparator in 15 trials (13 of the 20 active-only trials and 2 three-arm trials with placebo)'. The same misplacement is in the claim cl_can_med_chemo_nausea.

(a) 'Barthel ADL -0.58 (-1.73 to 0.56), 4 trials': in Table 2 that cell holds three unlabelled estimates beside Nabilone (2), Dronabinol (1), THC/CBD (1): -0.58 (-1.73 to 0.56), 0.23 (-0.13 to 0.59), -0.03 (-0.39 to 0.33). Figure 3 shows the same layout in the Ashworth row gives one estimate per product. -0.58, with a standard error of about 0.58, cannot be a pool that includes estimates with standard errors of about 0.18. So -0.58 is the nabilone estimate (2 trials), and no 4-trial Barthel estimate is reported. All three intervals include zero. (b) The note 'Table 2 still prints -0.11 (-0.23 to 0.02)': Figure 3 shows -0.11 (-0.23 to 0.02) is the nabiximols subtotal (Collin 2010, Collin 2007, Wade 2004, Berman 2007; 383 vs 337 patients), not an uncorrected overall. The other two Table 2 values are the dronabinol (-0.94, -2.37 to 0.49) and THC/CBD (-0.32, -1.59 to 0.95) arms of Zajicek 2003. The overall -0.12 (-0.24 to 0.01) is printed in Figure 3 as well as in the abstract and text. (c) '1244 patients' is Table 2's figure; Figure 3's overall row gives 590 + 544 = 1134.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: Figure 3 resolves the unlabelled cells. In the Ashworth row they are per-product estimates in the order of the cannabinoid column: nabiximols subtotal of 4 trials -0.11 (-0.23 to 0.02), THC/CBD -0.32 (-1.59 to 0.95) and dronabinol -0.94 (-2.37 to 0.49), the last two from the two arms of Zajicek 2003. Table 2 prints no overall; the corrected overall -0.12 (-0.24 to 0.01) is in Figure 3, the abstract and the text. So the issue is not that Table 2 kept an uncorrected overall: it never printed one. The Barthel row has the same layout, so its first value, -0.58 (-1.73 to 0.56), is the nabilone estimate (2 trials) and no 4-trial overall exists (see key finding 7). The table footnotes do exist, on the table image (View Large), but do not explain the cells. Consequence to add: -0.58 must not be cited as a pooled estimate of 4 trials; the card's key finding 7, its effect_sizes field and the claim cl_can_med_ms_spasticity all do so.

The Ashworth part is explained by Figure 3: one three-arm trial (Zajicek 2003) enters as two comparisons, dronabinol and THC/CBD, sharing its placebo group, so there are 6 comparisons for 5 trials. The consequence should say this double-counts that placebo group, against the review's stated rule; the effect on the estimate is negligible. The chronic-pain (30 products for 28 studies) and Barthel (2 nabilone trials against 1 nabilone study in the Spasticity section) parts stand unexplained.

Table 2's footnotes exist on the table image (View Large): abbreviations (CBM = cannabis based medicine), a (no glaucoma studies in the estimate; THC and cannabidiol were the interventions), b (what the outcome cell contains; follow-up not shown for all studies), c (definitions of the four GRADE grades). They give no reasons for individual GRADE ratings, so the consequence holds for the whole article, not only for the HTML. The Supplement 1 versus Supplement 2 inconsistency is confirmed (Results, 1st and 3rd paragraphs).

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low (provisional) follows from items 7 and 15, as the card says. Item 11 'yes' is defensible, but Figure 3 shows a three-arm trial entered twice with a shared placebo group, against the stated rule (negligible weight); the any-AE pool also mixes placebo and active comparators under one 'placebo' column (Figure 4), which the card already notes from Table 3's title.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. One qualification to point (5) and to the effect_sizes and selective_reporting fields: the summary gives no absolute numbers, but Figure 4 prints raw event counts for any adverse event (1438/1779 vs 1058/1710 across 29 studies; crude 81% vs 62%, editors' arithmetic), and Figure 2 prints the pain responder counts.

missed: Figures 2 to 4 (which the first reader could not load) were viewed by this reader as their View Large images. Figure 2's heterogeneity P values are misprinted: '.94' and '.64' should be .094 and .064 (recomputed from the printed counts; the I2 values 44.5% and 47.6% are right).

Figure 4: any adverse event, 29 studies with event counts 1438/1779 vs 1058/1710; patients 3489, against 3714 in Table 3 (an unexplained discrepancy of 225); the comparator column, headed placebo, includes active-comparator trials (for example levonantradol and nabilone antiemetic trials).
Figure 3's overall Ashworth row counts 590 + 544 = 1134 patients, against 1244 in Table 2 and in key finding 7.
The card's effect_sizes field repeats the Barthel error ('Barthel ADL -0.58 (-1.73 to 0.56), 4 trials') and the 'Table 2 prints -0.11' reading; both need the correction given under key finding 7.
validity_norms says Table 2's footnotes 'presumably give the reasons for each GRADE rating'; they do not (see reporting issue 7).

Table 2 gives the sleep-quality pool as 8 trials (539 patients) and the sleep-disturbance pool as 3 trials (1637 patients); for 3 trials against 8 the patient counts look transposed or wrong (minor; neither is cited in a claim).
